About This Book

LeetCode Patterns: The Recitation Method is organised around reduction, not around data structures. Every chapter answers one question: what is the smallest thing you must remember, such that a whole family of problems becomes a mechanical variation of it?

The organising principle is deliberately not the textbook taxonomy. A chapter called “BFS” tells you nothing you can memorise. A chapter called “Binary Search — The Boundary Rules” tells you that there are exactly two loop shapes and two midpoint formulas, that hi = mid implies the lower midpoint and lo = mid implies the upper one, and that violating this pairing is an infinite loop rather than a wrong answer. That is memorisable. That is what this book contains.

Where the problem set comes from

The index is built from 1151 problems that appear in at least one of 70 company interview sets, weighted so that tier-one companies (Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Netflix, Bloomberg, ByteDance, Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu) count triple. Difficulty, acceptance rate and topic tags come from LeetCode’s own problem catalogue. The frequency score printed beside each problem is a rough proxy for how often it is asked — not a probability.

How the numbers were derived

Problem identifiers are LeetCode’s frontend numbers, the ones that appear in the URL. This distinction matters more than it sounds: LeetCode’s public problem API returns an internal database id in its question_id field which diverges from the frontend number (the internal id of problem 704 is 792). Every identifier in this book was resolved through the frontend field and cross-checked against the official title and difficulty, and the build fails loudly if a reference does not resolve.

A note on premium problems

Problems marked with a dagger (†) are LeetCode Premium and are not freely accessible. They are included because they still appear in real interviews and the pattern is worth knowing, but you should not treat them as required practice.

This edition contains all 93 chapters across 17 parts, followed by the complete problem index in Appendix A.

Part I

The Method

Four short chapters that install the method: how to read this book, how to choose a pattern from the problem statement, the Python toolkit you should not have to re-derive, and the twenty templates that cover most of the thousand problems that follow.

Part I · The Method
Chapter 1

How to Use This Book

The Kernel

Read the kernel, type the template from memory, then only the delta matters. Never read a solution before you can write the template blind.

This book is written for a specific reader: someone who already writes code professionally, who has an interview in three to eight weeks, and who does not have two hundred hours to spend on a problem set. It assumes you can read Python and reason about complexity. It does not assume you have solved three hundred problems, and it does not spend pages on what an array is.

The organising bet is this: interview problems are not a thousand problems, they are about ninety patterns, and most of those patterns are three to ten lines of code plus a rule about boundaries. If you learn the rules, you can re-derive the code. If you only learn the code, you will be lost the moment the problem is dressed differently.

So every chapter in this book has the same five parts, in the same order, and each one has a job.

The Method

  1. Pass 1 (recall): read only the chapter’s Kernel and Boundary Rules, then close the book and type the template from memory.
  2. Pass 2 (recognition): read the Reduction Table. For each row, say out loud which single line of the template changes. If you cannot, you do not yet own the pattern.
  3. Pass 3 (drill): work the Index problems under a 25-minute timer each, writing only the changed lines, not the whole solution.
  4. Never memorise solutions. Memorise the kernel plus the boundary rule. Every worked example in this book is a re-derivation, not a recitation.

The five parts of a chapter

The Kernel is one sentence stating what every problem in the chapter collapses to. If you read nothing else, read this. A chapter whose kernel you cannot restate is a chapter you have not learned.

The Boundary Rules are the memorisable content. They are numbered because you should be able to recite them: rule three says hi = mid implies the lower midpoint. If you find yourself reasoning from first principles during an interview, you are spending attention you need for the problem itself.

The Template is the canonical code, written once, in the form you should be able to type from memory. It is deliberately not golfed — a template you cannot reproduce under pressure is worthless.

Worked Solutions show the template being applied, with the reasoning made explicit. Read these as derivations, not as answers to memorise.

The Index lists every remaining problem in the chapter’s family with a single sentence naming what changes in the template. This is the part that makes the book cover a thousand problems without becoming a thousand pages.

The three-pass method

Do not read this book front to back like a novel. Do not do the problems in chapter order either. Each chapter gets three passes, and the passes are deliberately separated in time.

  • Pass 1 — recall. Read only the Kernel and the Boundary Rules. Close the book. Type the template from memory. If you cannot, re-read and try again tomorrow; there is no point moving on.
  • Pass 2 — recognition. Read the Index table. For each row, say out loud which line of the template changes. You are not solving anything; you are training the recognition step, which is what actually fails in interviews.
  • Pass 3 — drill. Work the Drill Set with a timer. Write only the changed lines, not the whole solution, unless the problem is genuinely new. Twenty-five minutes per problem is the budget; past that, read the chapter again.

What to do when you are stuck

Being stuck has three distinct causes, and they have three distinct fixes. Diagnosing which one you have is most of the work.

  • You do not recognise the pattern. You read the problem and have no idea where to start. Fix: go back to chapter 2’s decision tree and work the four questions explicitly, out loud. Recognition is a skill and it is trained by Pass 2, not by solving more problems.
  • You recognise the pattern but cannot write the code. Fix: you learned the code instead of the rules. Re-read the Boundary Rules and re-derive the template from them.
  • You can write the code but it fails on edge cases. Fix: this is a boundary problem, and it is the most common failure of all. Before submitting, test the empty input, the single element, the two elements, and the all-equal input. In the binary search part that list is mandatory; in the rest of the book it is a habit worth building.

On memorising

There is a taboo against memorising in interview preparation, and it is misplaced. What is worth memorising is not solutions — it is rules. The difference matters: a memorised solution is worthless the moment the problem changes, whereas a memorised rule (if the branch moves lo to mid, the midpoint must round up) applies to every problem in the family and can be checked in two seconds.

The test of whether you have memorised a rule rather than a solution is whether you can state the failure mode it prevents. If you can say ‘this rule exists because otherwise the loop does not terminate on a two-element range’, you own it. If you can only say ‘this is what the template looks like’, you have memorised the wrong thing.

The principle

Memorise rules, derive code. A rule you can state with its failure mode is worth ten solutions you can only reproduce.

How the problem index was built

Every problem in this book appears in at least one of seventy company interview sets. The frequency score printed beside each problem weights tier-one companies (Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Netflix, Bloomberg, ByteDance, Tencent, Alibaba, Baidu) triple, so a problem asked by four tier-one companies outranks one asked by six smaller ones. Difficulty, acceptance rate and topic tags come from LeetCode’s own catalogue.

A dagger (†) marks LeetCode Premium problems. They are included because they genuinely appear in interviews, but you should not treat them as required practice.

The index table that ends every chapter has five columns. # is the LeetCode problem number, so you can find the problem instantly. Problem is the title as LeetCode spells it. Level is Easy, Medium or Hard. Asked is how many of the seventy company sets contain that problem — a rough proxy for how often it actually comes up, and the reason the rows appear in the order they do. What changes is the column that matters: it is the one or two edits that turn the chapter’s template into a solution for that specific problem. Read the index with a finger over that last column and try to predict the edit before you read it. That prediction, not the reading, is the practice.

Appendix A lists all of them in frequency order. Use it as a checklist, not a reading list.

Pitfalls

  1. Reading the book cover to cover. It is a reference with a reading order, not a narrative. If you read all ninety-three chapters without doing Pass 1 on any of them, you will finish with a warm feeling and no new capability.
  2. Doing Pass 3 first. Solving problems before you can state the rules teaches you the problems, not the pattern. It feels productive and it is the most common way to spend two hundred hours and still fail the interview.
  3. Skipping the Drill Set because you ‘already know’ a pattern. The patterns you already know are exactly the ones whose boundary cases you have quietly wrong.
  4. Treating the index tables as filler. They are the compression mechanism of the whole book: one sentence per problem is what lets a thousand problems fit in a book you can actually finish.
Part I · The Method
Chapter 2

The Pattern Recognition Decision Tree

The Kernel

Interview pattern choice is a 4-question funnel: what is the input shape, what is being asked, is there an ordering or monotonicity to exploit, and what is the constraint that forces the complexity class.

The Method

  1. Q1 — Input shape: array / string / linked list / tree / graph / matrix / interval set / nothing-but-a-number.
  2. Q2 — Ask shape: find one, count all, find the best, enumerate all, decide yes-no, or design a data structure.
  3. Q3 — Monotonicity: is the input sorted, or can a predicate be made monotone over a candidate answer? If yes, binary search is on the table.
  4. Q4 — Constraint: read the limits before you design. n <= 20 means bitmask or exponential. n <= 500 means O(n^2) DP or interval DP. n <= 10^4 means O(n log n). n <= 10^6 means O(n) or O(n log n) with a small constant. n <= 10^9 means O(log n) or O(sqrt n) — almost certainly binary search or maths.
Part I · The Method
Chapter 3

The Python Toolkit and Complexity Sheet

The Kernel

Python gives you a standard library that already implements half the patterns. Know which lines you never have to write again.

The Method

  1. Sorted insert / search: bisect_left, bisect_right — never hand-roll binary search when the array is already sorted.
  2. Top-K: heapq.nlargest(k, a) / heapq.nsmallest(k, a) for k << n; sorted(a)[-k:] for k close to n.
  3. Frequency: collections.Counter; ordered counts: defaultdict(int).
  4. Sliding-window maxima: collections.deque with maxlen where applicable.
  5. Cache: functools.lru_cache for memoised DP; functools.cache when the key space is small and unhashable args are not used.
  6. Iteration tools: itertools.accumulate for prefix sums, itertools.combinations / permutations / product for brute-force verification of your DP.
  7. Never mutate a list while iterating it; never use list.pop(0) in a loop (it is O(n)) — use a deque.
  8. Default arguments are evaluated once: never write def f(path=[]) in a backtracking signature.

Sequential Scans

Part II · Sequential Scans
Chapter 5

Two Pointers – Converging

The Kernel

One pointer at each end, both moving inward. Every problem here is the same while l < r: loop; only the move rule and the update rule differ.

This is the cheapest pattern in the book. There is one loop, two pointers, and a rule that says which one moves. Once the array is sorted, a pair is no longer something you search for — it is something you walk toward, and the walk is O(n) instead of O(n&sup2;).

The reason it works is a monotonicity argument, and you should be able to state it out loud in an interview. Put the smallest element on the left and the largest on the right. If their sum is too small, then the smallest element cannot be part of any valid pair — it is too small to pair with anything, including the largest value available. So discard it and move on. If the sum is too large, by the same argument the largest element cannot be in any valid pair. Every iteration removes one candidate permanently, which is what makes a single linear pass enough.

Everything else — 3Sum, 4Sum, closest pair, container with most water, palindrome checking — is that argument wearing a different costume. The chapter is short because there is genuinely only one idea in it.

32
Problems mapped
14
Easy
17

The Boundary Rules

Seven rules. Rule 1 and rule 2 are the loop itself; rule 3 is the precondition that makes the loop valid; rules 4 through 7 are the traps that separate a working answer from an accepted one.

  1. Loop condition is always while l < r (never <=) — a converging pair must have two distinct indices.
  2. Move exactly one pointer per iteration, decided by a comparison against the target. Moving both is the classic bug that silently skips candidates.
  3. If the array is not sorted and the problem is about pairs/triplets, sort first — the O(n log n) sort is what buys you the O(n) scan.
  4. After sorting, the index you get back is an index into the sorted array. If the problem asks for original indices, you must carry them.
  5. Dedup rule: skip a value only when it equals the previous kept value, and only while l < r. if l > start and a[l] == a[l-1]: continue.
  6. 3Sum is for i in range(n-2) wrapping a converging pair; the outer loop carries its own dedup and its own early exit if a[i] > 0: break.
  7. Container-with-most-water never needs sorting: the greedy move is move the shorter side, because the shorter side is the bottleneck.

The Template

There is one frame and one shell. The frame is the converging loop. The shell is the deduplication wrapper you need whenever the problem asks for a set of tuples rather than a single pair, which is where most submissions fail.

Memorise the frame. The shell you can rebuild each time from rule 5, as long as you remember that duplicates are skipped at the anchor and at the pointer separately — they are two different loops and they are both required.

# ------------------------------------------------- the frame
# Sorted array, one pointer at each end, both moving inward.

def two_sum_sorted(a, target):
    l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
    while l < r:            # never <= : a pair needs two indices
        s = a[l] + a[r]
        if s == target:
            return [l, r]
        if s < target:
            l += 1              # too small: low side is the bottleneck
        else:
            r -= 1              # too large: high side is the bottleneck
    return []               # no pair exists


# --------------------------------------------- the dedup shell
# Use whenever the answer is a SET of tuples, not one pair.

def three_sum(a):
    a.sort()                # sorting is what buys the O(n) scan
    out = []
    for i in range(len(a) - 2):
        if a[i] > 0:
            break           # sorted: no later triple can reach 0
        if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1]:
            continue        # skip a duplicate ANCHOR
        l, r = i + 1, len(a) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            if s == 0:
                out.append([a[i], a[l], a[r]])
                l += 1
                while l < r and a[l] == a[l - 1]:
                    l += 1  # skip duplicates of the value just used
            elif s < 0:
                l += 1
            else:
                r -= 1
    return out

Why moving both pointers at once is wrong

It is tempting to think that when the sum is too small you should advance l and retreat r, since neither endpoint looked right. That is a bug, and it is a silent one: it skips candidates without ever failing a test you would notice on a small example.

The monotonicity argument is what tells you the truth. When a[l] + a[r] is too small, a[l] is too small to pair with a[r] — the largest remaining value. That tells you nothing about a[r]. a[r] may well be the correct partner for some other element further in. Moving r discards it on no evidence.

So the rule is mechanical: exactly one pointer moves per iteration, and the comparison decides which. If you find yourself writing both, you have lost the invariant and the linear bound with it.

The two deduplication loops are not the same loop

In the three_sum shell there are two places duplicates are skipped, and they exist for different reasons. The outer check if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1]: continue skips a repeated anchor — if you have already produced every triple starting with the value 2, starting again at another 2 produces the same set.

The inner loop after a hit skips repeated partners — once you have emitted [-4, 2, 2], advancing l onto a second 2 would emit it again.

The trap is that the inner loop must be guarded by l < r, not by a fixed bound. Without it, a long run of equal values can walk l past r and produce a pair that reuses the same element twice, which is not a pair at all.

Worked Solutions

Eight problems. Each one is the frame with one decision changed, and the decision is named in the heading so you can find it again under pressure.

167Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
LC 167  ·  Medium  ·  asked by 6 companies  ·  AC 65.9%  ·  Array, Two Pointers, Binary Search
The Problem

You are given a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order.

Find two numbers such that they add up to a specific target number. Let these two numbers be numbers[index1] and numbers[index2] where 1 <= index1 < index2 <= numbers.length.

Return the indices of the two numbers index1 and index2 as an integer array [index1, index2] of length 2.

The tests are generated such that there is exactly one solution. You may not use the same element twice.

Your solution must use only constant extra space.

Example 1:

Input: numbers = [2,7,11,15], target = 9
Output: [1,2]

Explanation The sum of 2 and 7 is 9. Therefore, index<sub>1</sub> = 1, index<sub>2</sub> = 2. We return [1, 2].

Example 2:

Input: numbers = [2,3,4], target = 6
Output: [1,3]

Explanation The sum of 2 and 4 is 6. Therefore index<sub>1</sub> = 1, index<sub>2</sub> = 3. We return [1, 3].

Example 3:

Input: numbers = [-1,0], target = -1
Output: [1,2]

Explanation The sum of -1 and 0 is -1. Therefore index<sub>1</sub> = 1, index<sub>2</sub> = 2. We return [1, 2].

Constraints:

  • 2 <= numbers.length <= 3 * 104
  • -1000 <= numbers[i] <= 1000
  • numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order.
  • -1000 <= target <= 1000
  • The tests are generated such that there is exactly one solution.
Signature
def twoSum(numbers, target):   # -> integer[]

In one lineIn a sorted array, return the 1-indexed positions of the two numbers that add to target.

The insightThe frame in its purest form. The array is already sorted, so the only work is the comparison.

l starts at the smallest value and r at the largest. If the sum is too small, the smallest value cannot participate in any valid pair, so l advances. If too large, the largest value cannot, so r retreats. Each step discards one index for good.

The only thing the problem adds over the template is the off-by-one in the return: the statement is 1-indexed while Python is 0-indexed. That single + 1 on each end is the most commonly lost point on this problem.

def twoSum(numbers, target):
    l, r = 0, len(numbers) - 1
    while l < r:
        s = numbers[l] + numbers[r]
        if s == target:
            return [l + 1, r + 1]    # the statement is 1-indexed
        if s < target:
            l += 1
        else:
            r -= 1
    return []

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space. Compare the hash-map solution for Two Sum (1): O(n) time but O(n) space. Sortedness is what lets you drop the memory.

Pitfall

Returning [l, r] instead of [l + 1, r + 1].

Pitfall

Writing while l <= r. With <= the loop can settle on a single index and the function reports a number paired with itself.

Follow-up. “What if the array were not sorted?” Then either sort first — O(n log n) — or use the hash map from chapter 20. The converging frame requires order.

125Valid Palindrome
LC 125  ·  Easy  ·  asked by 6 companies  ·  AC 54.3%  ·  Two Pointers, String
The Problem

A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward. Alphanumeric characters include letters and numbers.

Given a string s, return trueif it is a palindrome, orfalseotherwise.

Example 1:

Input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
Output: true

Explanation “amanaplanacanalpanama” is a palindrome.

Example 2:

Input: s = "race a car"
Output: false

Explanation “raceacar” is not a palindrome.

Example 3:

Input: s = " "
Output: true

Explanation s is an empty string "" after removing non-alphanumeric characters. Since an empty string reads the same forward and backward, it is a palindrome.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s.length <= 2 * 105
  • s consists only of printable ASCII characters.
Signature
def isPalindrome(s):   # -> boolean

In one lineDecide whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters.

The insightSame frame, but the pointers must skip characters that do not count, and the skip loops need the same l < r guard as the outer loop.

The frame compares s[l] with s[r] and moves both inward — note that this is one of the few places both pointers move, because a palindrome match consumes both ends at once.

The new ingredient is the inner skip loops. A character that is not alphanumeric is invisible to the problem, so each pointer walks over it. The subtlety is that these loops must be guarded by l < r themselves. Without the guard, a string like ".," walks l off the end of the string and the next comparison reads out of range.

Normalise with .lower() at the point of comparison rather than rebuilding the string. Filtering into a new string is also correct but allocates O(n) memory for no reason.

def isPalindrome(s):
    l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
    while l < r:
        while l < r and not s[l].isalnum():
            l += 1
        while l < r and not s[r].isalnum():
            r -= 1
        if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower():
            return False
        l += 1
        r -= 1
    return True

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space. Each character is visited at most once by each pointer.

Pitfall

Omitting l < r inside the skip loops. This is the single most common failure on this problem.

Pitfall

Using s[l].isalpha() when the statement says alphanumeric — digits count, so "0P" is not a palindrome but "0P0" is.

Follow-up. “What if you may delete at most one character?” That is problem 680 below, and it is a one-line change with a trap.

153Sum
LC 15  ·  Medium  ·  asked by 19 companies  ·  AC 39.9%  ·  Array, Two Pointers, Sorting
The Problem

Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j, i != k, and j != k, and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0.

Notice that the solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

Example 1:

Input: nums = [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4]
Output: [[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]]

Explanation nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2] = (-1) + 0 + 1 = 0. nums[1] + nums[2] + nums[4] = 0 + 1 + (-1) = 0. nums[0] + nums[3] + nums[4] = (-1) + 2 + (-1) = 0. The distinct triplets are [-1,0,1] and [-1,-1,2]. Notice that the order of the output and the order of the triplets does not matter.

Example 2:

Input: nums = [0,1,1]
Output: []

Explanation The only possible triplet does not sum up to 0.

Example 3:

Input: nums = [0,0,0]
Output: [[0,0,0]]

Explanation The only possible triplet sums up to 0.

Constraints:

  • 3 <= nums.length <= 3000
  • -105 <= nums[i] <= 105
Signature
def threeSum(nums):   # -> list<list<integer>>

In one lineReturn every triple of distinct positions whose values sum to zero, with no repeated triples.

The insightSort, then wrap the converging frame in a loop over the anchor. The whole difficulty is the two deduplication loops, not the search.

Sorting does two things at once: it makes the inner converging scan valid, and it makes duplicates adjacent, which is what makes them skippable at all. Without the sort you cannot dedup in O(1) space per candidate.

The outer loop fixes nums[i] as the anchor and asks the inner frame for a pair summing to -nums[i]. Two early exits matter. if nums[i] > 0: break is valid because once the anchor is positive, every later anchor is larger and no triple can reach zero. The duplicate-anchor check if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue is what stops the same triple being emitted from different starting positions.

After a hit, l must skip past equal values. This is the second dedup loop, and it is guarded by l < r so it cannot overrun.

def threeSum(nums):
    nums.sort()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if nums[i] > 0:
            break                    # sorted: no later triple reaches 0
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
            continue                 # duplicate anchor
        l, r = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
            if s == 0:
                out.append([nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]])
                l += 1
                while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1]:
                    l += 1           # duplicate partner
            elif s < 0:
                l += 1
            else:
                r -= 1
    return out

Complexity. O(n&sup2;) time — O(n log n) to sort plus O(n) for each of n anchors. O(1) extra space beyond the output.

Pitfall

Keeping only one of the two dedup checks. With only the anchor check, a triple like [-1, 0, 1] is emitted once per duplicate partner; with only the partner check, it is emitted once per duplicate anchor.

Pitfall

Using a set of tuples instead of the two loops. It works, but it hides whether you understand the invariant, and interviewers ask.

Pitfall

Dropping the l < r guard inside the partner skip loop, which lets l run past r and reuse an element twice.

Follow-up. “And 4Sum?” Add a second anchor loop around the same shell — O(n&sup3;). The pattern does not change; only the nesting does.

11Container With Most Water
LC 11  ·  Medium  ·  asked by 9 companies  ·  AC 60.9%  ·  Array, Two Pointers, Greedy
The Problem

You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]).

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the most water.

Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

Notice that you may not slant the container.

Example 1:

[diagram omitted — see leetcode.com/problems/container-with-most-water/]

Input: height = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]
Output: 49

Explanation The above vertical lines are represented by array [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]. In this case, the max area of water (blue section) the container can contain is 49.

Example 2:

Input: height = [1,1]
Output: 1

Constraints:

  • n == height.length
  • 2 <= n <= 105
  • 0 <= height[i] <= 104
Signature
def maxArea(height):   # -> integer

In one lineGiven vertical lines at each index, choose two that with the x-axis hold the most water.

The insightThe only problem in the chapter that must not be sorted, because the answer depends on the original positions. The move rule is different too: move the shorter side.

The area is min(height[l], height[r]) * (r - l). Sorting would destroy the widths, so the array stays as it is and the frame runs on the original indices.

The move rule follows from the bottleneck argument. The shorter wall caps the area. Moving the taller wall inward can only reduce the width while the cap stays the same, so it can never improve. Moving the shorter wall is the only move that has any chance of finding a larger cap. This is the same “discard the endpoint that cannot participate” argument as the sorted case, applied to a different monotonicity.

Note what you do not do: you never look ahead. The greedy move is locally justified and globally optimal here, and the proof is the bottleneck argument above.

def maxArea(height):
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    best = 0
    while l < r:
        h = min(height[l], height[r])
        best = max(best, h * (r - l))
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            l += 1          # the shorter wall is the bottleneck
        else:
            r -= 1
    return best

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space. One comparison and one move per iteration.

Pitfall

Sorting the array first. The area depends on index distance, so sorting changes the answer — this is the trap that catches people who have just learned 3Sum.

Pitfall

Moving the taller wall. It looks harmless and is wrong on inputs where the optimum needs both walls from one half.

Pitfall

Computing h * (r - l) with h = height[l] only, instead of the minimum of the two.

Follow-up. “Prove the greedy move.” This is the standard exchange argument: any solution that keeps the shorter wall and discards the taller one is dominated by the move the algorithm makes.

163Sum Closest
LC 16  ·  Medium  ·  asked by 7 companies  ·  AC 47.4%  ·  Array, Two Pointers, Sorting
The Problem

You are given an integer array nums of length n and an integer target.

Find three integers at distinct indices in nums such that the sum is closest to target.

Return the sum of the three integers.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution.

Example 1:

Input: nums = [-1,2,1,-4], target = 1
Output: 2

Explanation The sum that is closest to the target is 2. (-1 + 2 + 1 = 2).

Example 2:

Input: nums = [0,0,0], target = 1
Output: 0

Explanation The sum that is closest to the target is 0. (0 + 0 + 0 = 0).

Constraints:

  • 3 <= nums.length <= 500
  • -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000
  • -104 <= target <= 104
Signature
def threeSumClosest(nums, target):   # -> integer

In one lineFind the triple whose sum is closest to a target.

The insightThe 3Sum shell with the equality test replaced by a running best. No deduplication is needed, because the answer is a single number rather than a set of tuples.

This is the clearest demonstration that the two dedup loops in 3Sum are not part of the frame — they belong to the output shape. Here the output is one integer, so both loops vanish and the code gets shorter.

The frame is unchanged: too small advances l, too large retreats r. The only addition is that every candidate is compared against the best so far, since the exact target may never be hit.

The early return when s == target is worth keeping: an exact hit is optimal and no further work can improve it.

def threeSumClosest(nums, target):
    nums.sort()
    best = nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2]
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        l, r = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
            if abs(s - target) < abs(best - target):
                best = s
            if s < target:
                l += 1
            elif s > target:
                r -= 1
            else:
                return target        # exact hit: cannot be beaten
    return best

Complexity. O(n&sup2;) time, O(1) space. The early return makes the common case much faster than the bound suggests.

Pitfall

Seeding best with a sentinel like float('inf') and then returning it when the array is short. Seed from the first triple instead — the array always has at least three elements.

Pitfall

Forgetting the exact-hit early return, which is not a correctness bug but is the difference between passing and looking like you know the problem.

Follow-up. “Closest pair in a sorted array?” Same running-best idea with the plain frame, no anchor loop.

42Trapping Rain Water
LC 42  ·  Hard  ·  asked by 18 companies  ·  AC 68.2%  ·  Array, Two Pointers, Dynamic Programming, Stack
The Problem

Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.

Example 1:

[diagram omitted — see leetcode.com/problems/trapping-rain-water/]

Input: height = [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1]
Output: 6

Explanation The above elevation map (black section) is represented by array [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1]. In this case, 6 units of rain water (blue section) are being trapped.

Example 2:

Input: height = [4,2,0,3,2,5]
Output: 9

Constraints:

  • n == height.length
  • 1 <= n <= 2 * 104
  • 0 <= height[i] <= 105
Signature
def trap(height):   # -> integer

In one lineGiven an elevation map, compute how much rain it traps.

The insightThe hardest problem in the chapter, and it is still the same frame. The water above any bar is min(left_max, right_max) - height, and the converging scan can supply that minimum without ever building either array.

The straightforward solution computes two prefix arrays — the tallest bar to the left of each index and the tallest to the right — then sums min(left, right) - height. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, and it is a perfectly good answer.

The two-pointer version removes the arrays. The key observation: when height[l] < height[r], the water above l is determined entirely by left_max, because there is a bar at r at least as tall as height[l] somewhere to the right, which is enough to guarantee right_max >= height[l]. So min(left_max, right_max) == left_max and you can settle l immediately without knowing right_max at all.

That is the whole trick, and it is worth stating precisely: you never need both maxima, only the one on the side of the shorter bar. The loop advances whichever side is shorter and settles that index permanently.

def trap(height):
    if not height:
        return 0
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            water += left_max - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])
            water += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return water

Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) space. Strictly better than the prefix-array solution on memory, and the version an interviewer is hoping you reach.

Pitfall

Comparing height[l] with height[r] and then using the wrong maximum. The rule is: whichever bar is shorter, its side’s maximum is the binding constraint. Swap them and the answer is wrong on asymmetric inputs.

Pitfall

Updating left_max after accumulating instead of before, which adds a negative term at every new maximum.

Pitfall

Forgetting the empty-input guard, which makes l and r invalid on an empty array.

Follow-up. “What about the 2-D version?” Problem 407. It needs a heap rather than two pointers — see chapter 32 — because there is no single pair of maxima that bounds the water.

680Valid Palindrome II
LC 680  ·  Easy  ·  asked by 7 companies  ·  AC 44.8%  ·  Two Pointers, String, Greedy
The Problem

Given a string s, return true if thescan be palindrome after deleting at most one character from it.

Example 1:

Input: s = "aba"
Output: true

Example 2:

Input: s = "abca"
Output: true

Explanation You could delete the character ‘c’.

Example 3:

Input: s = "abc"
Output: false

Constraints:

  • 1 <= s.length <= 105
  • s consists of lowercase English letters.
Signature
def validPalindrome(s):   # -> boolean

In one lineDecide whether a string is a palindrome after deleting at most one character.

The insightRun the frame; at the first mismatch, the answer is the OR of the two possible deletions. Only one branch can be right, and you must try both.

The frame advances while the characters match. The moment they differ, exactly one of two things must be true: the left character is the extra one, or the right character is. So you check the remaining substring both ways and accept if either works.

The trap is thinking you can decide which one to delete from the local comparison. You cannot. Given "abca" mismatching at the outer pair, both branches must be tested, because the surrounding context decides it and you have not looked at the surroundings yet.

Factor the plain check into a helper. The outer loop runs once and calls the helper at most twice, which is why the total work is still linear — each helper call scans a substring, and there are only two of them.

def validPalindrome(s):
    def ok(i, j):
        while i < j:
            if s[i] != s[j]:
                return False
            i += 1
            j -= 1
        return True

    l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
    while l < r:
        if s[l] != s[r]:
            return ok(l + 1, r) or ok(l, r - 1)
        l += 1
        r -= 1
    return True

Complexity. O(n) time — the outer loop plus at most two linear scans. O(1) space beyond the recursion-free helper.

Pitfall

Trying only one branch, e.g. always skipping s[l]. Which character is the extra one depends on the rest of the string, not on the mismatch itself.

Pitfall

Recursing instead of using a helper and accidentally making it exponential, because each mismatch can spawn two more.

Pitfall

Returning False after both branches fail but forgetting that the loop must also return True when no mismatch is found at all.

Follow-up. “At most k deletions?” That is the two-sequence DP of chapter 62 — the greedy two-branch trick works only for k = 1.

977Squares of a Sorted Array
LC 977  ·  Easy  ·  asked by 5 companies  ·  AC 74.2%  ·  Array, Two Pointers, Sorting
The Problem

Given an integer array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number sorted in non-decreasing order.

Example 1:

Input: nums = [-4,-1,0,3,10]
Output: [0,1,9,16,100]

Explanation After squaring, the array becomes [16,1,0,9,100]. After sorting, it becomes [0,1,9,16,100].

Example 2:

Input: nums = [-7,-3,2,3,11]
Output: [4,9,9,49,121]

Constraints:

  • 1 <= nums.length <=104
  • -104 <= nums[i] <= 104
  • nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
Signature
def sortedSquares(nums):   # -> integer[]

In one lineGiven a sorted array, return the squares of its elements in sorted order.

The insightThe largest square is at one of the two ends, so fill the output from the back while converging inward.

The array is sorted, but its squares are not: a large negative number at the left can square to more than a large positive at the right. So the usual “smallest first” order is broken.

The fix is to reverse the direction of the fill. The largest square is always at one of the two ends, because that is where the largest magnitudes live. Compare abs(nums[l]) with abs(nums[r]), take the bigger square, place it at the current back position, and advance that pointer. The output fills from the last index down to zero.

Note that both pointers move inward but only one per iteration, exactly as rule 2 requires. Writing into a preallocated list from the back avoids the insert(0, ...) that would make the solution quadratic.

def sortedSquares(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [0] * n
    l, r = 0, n - 1
    for k in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        if abs(nums[l]) > abs(nums[r]):
            out[k] = nums[l] * nums[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            out[k] = nums[r] * nums[r]
            r -= 1
    return out

Complexity. O(n) time, O(n) space for the output. Beats the obvious sort-the-squares approach, which is O(n log n).

Pitfall

Using nums[l] nums[l] > nums[r] nums[r] without abs. The squares of negatives compare wrongly if you forget.

Pitfall

Writing to the front with out.append(...) and then reversing, which is correct but obscures the direction of the fill.

Pitfall

Using insert(0, x), which is O(n) per call and quietly turns a linear solution into a quadratic one.

Follow-up. “Why is the maximum always at an end?” Because x&sup2; is monotone in |x|, and the extremes of |x| are at the ends of a sorted array.

Pitfalls

  1. Sorting a problem that depends on original positions. Rule 3 tells you to sort for pair problems. It does not apply to Container With Most Water (11), Trapping Rain Water (42) or Boats to Save People (881) — in the first two the answer is the distance between indices, and sorting destroys it. Ask whether the answer depends on positions before you call .sort().
  2. Moving both pointers in one iteration. The comparison justifies discarding exactly one endpoint. Moving both discards a candidate on no evidence and silently skips valid answers.
  3. Writing while l <= r. A pair needs two distinct indices. With <=, the loop can settle on l == r and pair an element with itself.
  4. Keeping only one of the two dedup loops. In 3Sum they are separate for a reason: one skips duplicate anchors, the other skips duplicate partners. Removing either produces repeated triples.
  5. The partner skip loop without its own l < r guard. A long run of equal values walks l past r, and the next comparison reads the same element twice or goes out of range.
  6. Forgetting that sorting costs O(n log n). The frame is O(n), but the problem is not linear unless the input arrives sorted. Say the bound as O(n log n) when you sort.
  7. Reaching for two pointers when n is tiny. Maximum Strong Pair XOR (2932) has n <= 50; brute force is the intended answer and the converging frame does not apply at all.
  8. Assuming the frame needs a for loop. The frame is a while l < r. If you find yourself indexing with for i in range(...), you are probably in a different pattern.

Drill Set

Thirty problems, ordered so that each adds exactly one idea to the previous. The first eight are the frame alone; 15 and 16 introduce the dedup shell; 42 is the only one that needs an argument rather than a substitution.

Do them without looking at the template. If a problem takes more than eight minutes, stop, re-read the boundary rule it violates, and restart from the frame.

Target: thirty minutes for the first twelve, forty for the rest. If you finish faster you are guessing rather than applying the rules, and the mistakes will surface under interview pressure.

Part II · Sequential Scans
Chapter 6

Two Pointers – Same Direction

The Kernel

One slow write-pointer, one fast read-pointer. The slow pointer delineates the answer prefix; the fast pointer scans everything else. This is the in-place filtering pattern.

22
Problems mapped
14
Easy
8
Medium
0
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The write pointer only advances when you keep an element. Everything before w is finished output; everything at or after f is unread.
  2. for f in range(n) + if keep: a[w] = a[f]; w += 1 is the whole shape. Never write a second loop.
  3. Deleting duplicates in place: compare against a[w-1] (the last kept value), not a[f-1] — that is the single most common mistake.
  4. When at most two copies are allowed, the guard becomes if w < 2 or a[f] != a[w-2].
  5. Merge from the back when the destination array has spare capacity at the end (88): w = m + n - 1, and always copy the larger of the two tails so you never overwrite unread data.
  6. Fast/slow pointers on a linked list are the same idea applied to a non-indexable structure; see the Linked List part.
  7. Cycle detection on an array-as-functional-graph uses Floyd’s tortoise and hare: slow = f(slow); fast = f(f(fast)) and the meeting point is not the entry point — you need a second pass to find the entry.

Chapter 7

Sliding Window – Fixed Size

The Kernel

A window of exactly k elements slides right by one. Add the entering element, remove the leaving element, evaluate the invariant. Nothing else ever happens.

23
Problems mapped
7
Easy
15
Medium
1
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Initialise by consuming the first k elements, then loop for r in range(k, n). Do not try to fold the first window into the loop — it costs you a branch on every iteration.
  2. The leaving index is always r - k. If you ever find yourself writing r - k + 1 you have mixed up a fixed and a variable window.
  3. For ‘anagram in a string’, compare two Counters of size 26, or keep a single matches counter and increment it only when a bucket hits zero. Rebuilding the Counter each step turns O(n) into O(26n) with a big constant.
  4. For ‘at most k distinct in a fixed window’ use the variable-window template instead — a fixed window whose validity can fail mid-window is a variable window in disguise.
  5. Fixed-window maxima are NOT a sliding window chapter problem; they need a monotonic deque (chapter 28). Recognise the difference: sum/count invariants are O(1) to update, max/min invariants are not.

Chapter 8

Sliding Window – Variable Size

The Kernel

Grow the right edge unconditionally; shrink the left edge only while the window is invalid. The window is always the maximal valid window ending at r.

29
Problems mapped
2
Easy
23
Medium
4
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The loop is for r in range(n): then while <invalid>: remove(a[l]); l += 1. The inner while is what makes it O(n) — each element enters and leaves exactly once.
  2. Never write if where the inner loop needs while. An if silently allows an invalid window to persist and is the number-one cause of wrong answers in this chapter.
  3. Decide up front which of the two variants you need: (a) longest valid window — shrink until valid, then record r - l + 1; (b) shortest window satisfying a target — shrink while valid, recording before each shrink, and grow only when invalid.
  4. For ‘longest’, the answer is recorded after the shrink loop. For ‘shortest’, the answer is recorded inside the shrink loop, before the pointer moves. Swapping these two is the second most common bug.
  5. The state you maintain must be incrementally updatable in O(1): a count, a sum, a frequency map, a count of distinct keys, or a count of ‘already satisfied’ constraints. If it is not, you have the wrong window definition.
  6. Longest substring without repeating characters is the archetype: the window is invalid exactly when freq[c] > 1, and the fix is to move l until that stops being true — not to move l to last[c] + 1 unless you also clear the intermediate characters.
  7. At-most-K distinct problems are ‘longest’ problems. Exactly-K distinct problems are at_most(K) - at_most(K-1); see chapter 9.

Chapter 9

Sliding Window – At Most K Reduces to Exactly K

The Kernel

Counting windows with an exact property is hard; counting windows with an at most property is a five-line scan. So compute the easy one twice.

14

The Boundary Rules

  1. exactly(K) = at_most(K) - at_most(K-1). This identity is the whole chapter; recognise it and the problem collapses.
  2. at_most(K) is a pure variable window: grow r, shrink l while the count of distinct keys exceeds K, and add r - l + 1 to the answer. r - l + 1 is the number of valid windows ending at r.
  3. Binary subarrays with sum K (930) uses the same identity on the numeric sum, with a non-negative array. Non-negativity is what makes the window monotone; with negatives you must use prefix sums + hash (chapter 15).
  4. Subarrays with K Different Integers (992) and Count Number of Nice Subarrays (1248) are the same two-call shape. For 1248 the ‘distinct keys’ count becomes ‘count of odd numbers’.
  5. Do not try to track the number of windows with exactly K in a single pass with a third pointer unless you can prove it — the two-call identity is always correct and always fast enough.
