Chapter 35

Linked List – Fast and Slow Pointers

The Kernel

Two pointers at different speeds. If there is a cycle they meet; if not, the fast one hits the end. The offset between them also locates the middle, or the kth node from the end.

16
Problems mapped
6
Easy
10
Medium
0
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Cycle detection (141): while fast and fast.next: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if slow is fast: return True. The fast and fast.next guard is mandatory — fast.next.next on a one-node list raises.
  2. Cycle entry (142): after they meet, put one pointer back at head and advance both one step at a time. They meet at the entry. The maths is 2(a + b) = a + b + c + b giving a = c — be able to state that identity, because interviewers ask why it works.
  3. Middle node (876): while fast and fast.next: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next. For an even-length list this returns the second middle. If the problem wants the first middle, start fast = head.next.
  4. The first-vs-second-middle distinction matters enormously in 143 and 234, where a wrong choice silently produces the wrong interleaving.
  5. Nth from end (19): advance fast by n + 1 from a dummy, then move both until fast is None. slow is now the node before the target, which is what you need to delete it. Advancing by n instead of n + 1 puts you on the target itself and you cannot unlink it.
  6. Intersection of two lists (160): walk both with wraparound — a = a.next if a else headB. After at most m + n steps they align at the intersection, or both become None together. No length computation needed.
  7. Sort List (148) uses fast/slow to split, then merges. The fast/slow here must find the first middle to avoid infinite recursion on two-element lists.
  8. The same technique applies to non-linked structures: Happy Number (202) and Find the Duplicate Number (287) treat an array as a functional graph. 287 is the most important non-list application — it is a cycle-entry problem with a binary-search alternative, and interviewers like hearing both.

Linked List – Merge, Sort, and Reorder

The Kernel

Merge two sorted lists is a dummy-head while-loop. Sort a list is merge sort, which is the only O(n log n) sort that works on a linked list without random access.

17
Problems mapped
1
Easy
15
Medium
1

The Boundary Rules

  1. Merge shape. dummy + tail pointer; while a and b: pick the smaller; tail = tail.next; then tail.next = a or b to drain the rest. The final or is the elegant drain and always works because at most one list is non-empty.
  2. Use <= not < when merging to keep the merge stable. It rarely changes the answer, but it is the correct choice and interviewers notice.
  3. Merge Two Sorted Lists (21) is the base case of Merge k Sorted Lists (23). Sort List (148) is 21 plus a fast/slow split plus recursion. Three problems, one template, increasing depth.
  4. Sort List must be merge sort, not quicksort: quicksort needs random access to pick a good pivot, and a linked list does not have it. Saying this in an interview is worth more than the code.
  5. Add Two Numbers (2) is a merge with carry. The carry is a third loop variable, and after the loop you must handle a trailing carry (if carry: tail.next = ListNode(1)).
  6. Add Two Numbers II (445) reverses the inputs — either reverse the lists first, or use two stacks. Stacks are cleaner and avoid mutating the input, which the problem may forbid.
  7. Partition List (86) is two dummy heads (a less list and a ge list) joined at the end. Two dummies beats trying to do it in place.
  8. Odd Even Linked List (328) is also two chains, interleaved by index parity, then joined. Same shape as 86.
  9. Reorder List (143) is 876 + 206 + 21 composed. If you have internalised the three templates, this problem is 15 lines.
  10. Copy List with Random Pointer (138) belongs here by adjacency: the O(1)-space solution interleaves cloned nodes into the original list (a -> a' -> b -> b') so the random pointers can be resolved by node.next.random = node.random.next. That interleaving trick is worth memorising; the dict-based O(n)-space solution is the safe fallback.

Linked List – Dummy Head, Deletion, and Design

The Kernel

Almost every linked-list bug is a null-pointer or a head-replacement edge case. A dummy head removes the second category entirely; careful guard clauses remove the first.

19
Problems mapped
4
Easy
14
Medium
1
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Rule: if the head can be removed or replaced, use a dummy. 203, 82, 83, 19, 21, 86, 92, 25, 148, 138 — all of them.
  2. Delete by value (203): while cur.next: if cur.next.val == v: cur.next = cur.next.next else: cur = cur.next. Do not advance cur in the delete branch — you would skip a consecutive duplicate.
  3. Delete all duplicates (82): when a duplicate run is detected, walk to the end of the run first, then unlink the whole run. Do not unlink node by node.
  4. Delete a node given only that node (237): copy the next node’s value into the current node and unlink the next. It is a trick, and it does not work for the last node — the problem guarantees it will not be the last node.
  5. Design Linked List (707) needs addAtHead, addAtTail, addAtIndex, deleteAtIndex. Use a dummy head plus a size field; deriving the size by walking is O(n) and will fail the follow-up.
  6. Circular queue (622) and circular deque (641) are easier with a fixed-size list and two index pointers than with actual nodes. Do not over-engineer.
  7. LRU Cache (146) is the flagship linked-list design problem: dummy head and dummy tail, add_to_head and remove_node as two helpers. Write the helpers first and the rest becomes trivial.
  8. Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List (430) is a stack-based depth-first walk, or a recursive helper that returns the tail of the flattened segment. Both are acceptable; the iterative stack version has no recursion depth risk.
  9. The universal debugging habit for this chapter: draw three nodes and trace your pointer updates by hand before running anything. Linked-list bugs are almost never logical — they are ordering bugs in the assignment sequence.

Trees. One recursive skeleton, two directions of information flow, and the hybrid that computes a diameter while returning a height.

Part IX · Trees
Chapter 38

Tree Traversal – The Recursive Skeleton

The Kernel

Every recursive tree function is the same six lines: base case on None, recurse left, recurse right, combine. The only question is where you put the combine step — before (preorder), between (inorder), or after (postorder).

52
Problems mapped
29
Easy
22
Medium
1
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The skeleton. def f(node): if not node: return BASE; L = f(node.left); R = f(node.right); return COMBINE(node, L, R). Write it once and you own a hundred tree problems.
  2. Base case first, always. if not node: return <identity> where the identity is 0 for sums and depths, None for nodes, [] for lists, True for boolean properties.
  3. Where you place the work decides the order. Work before the recursive calls = preorder (root first). Work between them = inorder (only meaningful for BSTs). Work after = postorder (children first, needed whenever a parent’s answer depends on its children’s answers).
  4. Preorder (144) is for top-down information: carrying a bound, a prefix, a depth, or a path down the tree.
  5. Postorder (145) is for bottom-up information: heights, subtree sums, subtree validity. If the parent needs a value returned by the children, it is postorder.
  6. Inorder (94) on a BST gives sorted order. That single fact answers Validate BST (98), Kth Smallest (230), BST Iterator (173), Minimum Absolute Difference (530), Find Mode (501), Recover BST (99) and Convert BST to Greater Tree (538).
  7. Invert Binary Tree (226) is node.left, node.right = f(node.right), f(node.left). The tuple assignment is not a party trick — it avoids the classic bug of overwriting node.left before recursing on it.
  8. Same Tree (100) is the base-case pair: if not p and not q: return True; if not p or not q: return False. Write both guards, in that order.
  9. Symmetric Tree (101) is Same Tree with mirrored arguments: mirror(a.left, b.right) and mirror(a.right, b.left).
  10. Subtree of Another Tree (572) is is_same(root, sub) or is_subtree(root.left, sub) or is_subtree(root.right, sub). O(n*m) worst case; the O(n) answer uses tree hashing and is a nice follow-up.
  11. Merge Two Binary Trees (617) and Leaf-Similar Trees (872) are the same pairwise-recursion shape applied to two trees at once.
  12. N-ary trees (589, 590, 559, 429) are identical with a loop over node.children replacing the two explicit recursions.
  13. Recursion depth is O(h). For a degenerate tree of 10^5 nodes Python’s default limit of 1000 will raise RecursionError — mention this, and know that sys.setrecursionlimit is the fix, or write it iteratively.

Chapter 39

Tree Traversal – Iterative and Morris

The Kernel

An explicit stack replaces the call stack. Preorder is trivial; inorder is ‘go left as far as possible, then visit, then go right’; postorder is preorder with the children swapped and the result reversed.

22
Problems mapped
9
Easy
12
Medium
1
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Inorder iterative — memorise this one shape. stack = []; cur = root; while stack or cur: while cur: stack.append(cur); cur = cur.left; cur = stack.pop(); visit(cur); cur = cur.right.
  2. Preorder iterative is the inorder shape with visit moved before the left descent, or the simple ‘push right then left’ stack version.
  3. Postorder iterative is preorder with left and right pushed in swapped order, then result.reverse(). That one-line reduction is far safer than the two-stack or the ‘last visited’ variants.
  4. BST Iterator (173) is the inorder loop frozen mid-flight: keep the stack as instance state, and next() pops one node and pushes its entire left spine. hasNext() is bool(stack). This is the single most asked follow-up on the inorder template.
  5. Morris traversal achieves O(1) space by threading the rightmost node of the left subtree back to the current node. Know that it exists and that it is O(n) time, O(1) space — you will almost never be asked to write it, but ‘Morris traversal gives O(1) space’ is a strong answer to ‘can you do better on space?’.
  6. Kth Smallest in a BST (230) is inorder with a counter and an early exit. Iterative is better than recursive here precisely because you can stop early — recursion cannot.
  7. Validate BST (98) has three solutions: inorder-must-be-increasing (cleanest), recursion with (low, high) bounds (most instructive), and Morris with O(1) space. The bounds version is the one to write under pressure: f(node, lo, hi) with if not (lo < node.val < hi): return False.
  8. Never validate a BST by comparing only with the immediate children. [5,1,4,null,null,3,6] passes the naive test and is not a BST. This is the trap the problem is built on.

Tree BFS – The Level Order Family

The Kernel

A queue plus a ‘process the whole level before moving on’ loop. The level boundary is what makes BFS different from DFS, and it is what every level-based question actually asks for.

18
Problems mapped
2
Easy
15
Medium
1
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The level-boundary idiom. while q: for _ in range(len(q)): node = q.popleft(); .... Capturing len(q) before the inner loop is what separates levels. Iterating while q without it flattens the tree and breaks every level question.
  2. Level Order (102) collects each level into its own list; Level Order II (107) is the same list reversed; Zigzag (103) reverses the level when level % 2 == 1.
  3. Right Side View (199) is the last node of each level — level[-1]. Average of Levels (637) is sum(level) / len(level). Largest Value in Each Row (515) is max(level). Bottom Left (513) is the first node of the last level.
  4. Populating Next Right Pointers (116, 117) can be done with a queue in O(n) space, but the O(1)-space solution uses the already-built next pointers of the level above as a linked list. The O(1) version is the follow-up and is worth knowing.
  5. Maximum Width of Binary Tree (662) requires position indices: left child 2i, right child 2i+1. Without indices, nulls between real nodes are invisible and the width is wrong. Beware of integer overflow in other languages; Python is safe.
  6. Vertical Order Traversal (314, 987) needs a column index carried through the BFS (or DFS) plus a sort. 314 groups by column only; 987 also sorts by row and value, which is why it is the harder of the two.
  7. Minimum Depth (111) must use BFS, not DFS, if you want the early exit — and it must test if not node.left and not node.right rather than if not node.left or not node.right, or a node with one child terminates the search incorrectly.
  8. All Nodes Distance K (863) is BFS on the tree after adding parent pointers — an undirected graph traversal in disguise. That reframing is the whole insight.
  9. Use BFS when the question mentions a level, a depth, a shortest path, or nearest. Use DFS when it mentions a path, a subtree, or an aggregate.

Chapter 41

Tree DFS – Top-Down vs Bottom-Up

The Kernel

Two directions of information flow. Top-down passes an accumulated context into the recursion; bottom-up returns a summary out of it. Naming which one you need is 80% of solving a tree problem.

34
Problems mapped
5
Easy
27
Medium
2
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Top-down: the function takes extra parameters representing the path so far (depth, running_sum, lo/hi bounds, prefix). The answer is updated at the leaves. Signature: f(node, state).
  2. Bottom-up: the function returns a value that summarises the subtree (height, sum, is_valid, best). The answer is computed from the children’s returns. Signature: f(node) -> summary.
  3. The hybrid — and this is the key insight. When the answer is a quantity that the parent also needs (a height, a sum, a longest chain), the function must do two things at once: update a nonlocal best and return the value the parent needs. The best and the return value are different quantities.
  4. Diameter of Binary Tree (543) is the canonical hybrid: return 1 + max(left_h, right_h) to the parent, but update best = max(best, left_h + right_h) locally. Confusing the two gives the height instead of the diameter — the most common tree bug in existence.
  5. Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (124) is 543 with weights: return node.val + max(0, left, right) and update best = max(best, node.val + left + right). The max(0, ...) clamps negative branches, which is the whole difficulty of the problem.
  6. Balanced Binary Tree (110) is 543 with a validity flag: return -1 as a sentinel for ‘unbalanced’ instead of adding a second pass. The sentinel-return trick turns O(n log n) into O(n).
  7. Longest Univalue Path (687) and Longest ZigZag Path (1372) are 543 with a conditional on whether the child can be extended.
  8. Distribute Coins (979) returns the excess/deficit to the parent and adds abs(excess) to the moves. Binary Tree Cameras (968) returns a three-state enum. Both are bottom-up with a non-obvious return value — state what the return value means before coding.
  9. Count Good Nodes (1448) is pure top-down: pass the running maximum down, count at the node.
  10. Path Sum III (437) is top-down with a prefix-sum hash: carry the running sum and a dict of seen prefix sums, exactly like chapter 15. Recognising that the tree path problem is a prefix-sum problem is a high-value reduction.
  11. Sum Root to Leaf Numbers (129) and Path Sum II (113) are top-down with a path list; 113 needs path.copy() on append, because the list is mutated on the way back up.
  12. The back-tracking rule for path lists. Append before recursing, path.pop() after. If you forget the pop you get exponential memory and wrong answers.

Chapter 42

BST – Exploiting the Ordering

The Kernel

A BST gives you binary search for free. The two tools are the (low, high) bounds carried down the recursion, and the inorder traversal that yields sorted order.

37
Problems mapped
8
Easy
27
Medium
2
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Bounds, not parent comparison. f(node, lo, hi) with if not (lo < node.val < hi): return False then recurse with (lo, node.val) and (node.val, hi). Start with (-inf, +inf). Comparing only against the parent is the classic wrong answer.
  2. Insert (701): recurse by comparison; when you hit None, create the node. Return the (possibly new) root and assign it back: node.left = insert(node.left, val).
  3. Search (700): while node: if val < node.val: node = node.left elif val > node.val: node = node.right else: return node. Iterative is shorter than recursive here.
  4. Delete (450) is the only hard one. Three cases: no child -> return None; one child -> return that child; two children -> replace the value with the inorder successor (leftmost of the right subtree) and then delete that successor from the right subtree. Say ‘inorder successor’ out loud — interviewers are listening for it.
  5. LCA in a BST (235): walk down from the root. While both targets are on the same side, move there; the first node where they split is the answer. O(h), no recursion needed.
  6. Kth smallest (230), mode (501), minimum absolute difference (530), recover BST (99), greater tree (538) are all ‘inorder gives sorted order’. For 99, the two swapped nodes appear as two adjacent inversions in the inorder sequence.
  7. Unique BSTs (96) is Catalan-number DP, not a tree traversal: dp[i] = sum(dp[j] dp[i-1-j]). Unique BSTs II (95) is the recursive enumeration version. Recognise that these are counting and construction* problems wearing a BST costume.
  8. Construct from traversal (105, 106, 889, 1008, 654): preorder gives the root, inorder gives the split point. For 105, index the inorder array into a dict so each lookup is O(1) — without it you are at O(n^2).
  9. Construct BST from Preorder (1008) needs no inorder because the BST property supplies the split: use bounds, not a lookup.
  10. Balance a BST (1382) is ‘inorder to sorted list, then build a balanced tree from the middle’ — two templates composed.
  11. Closest value (270) and inorder successor (285) are bound walks: keep a best and update it as you descend.

Part IX · Trees
Chapter 43

Tree – Path Problems

The Kernel

A path is a sequence from an ancestor to a descendant (or through a node, for ‘any path’). Root-to-leaf paths are top-down with a path list; ‘any path’ problems are the hybrid from chapter 41.

22
Problems mapped
5
Easy
15
Medium
2
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Root-to-leaf with a list. Append node.val, recurse, then path.pop(). At a leaf, result.append(path.copy()) — copy() is mandatory, otherwise every entry in the result aliases the same mutable list and you finish with n copies of the last path.
  2. Root-to-leaf with a sum. Carry the remaining target (target - node.val) rather than accumulating, so the leaf test is target == 0.
  3. Path Sum (112) is boolean; Path Sum II (113) collects the paths; Sum Root to Leaf Numbers (129) accumulates 10 cur + node.val; Sum of Root To Leaf Binary Numbers (1022) accumulates cur 2 + node.val. Same walk, different accumulator.
  4. Path Sum III (437) is not root-to-leaf: it counts any downward path. The answer is the prefix-sum hash from chapter 15 applied to the DFS path: seen = {0: 1}, cur += node.val, ans += seen.get(cur - target, 0), recurse, then seen[cur] -= 1 on the way back. The decrement on the way back is the whole trick — it is the DFS equivalent of path.pop().
  5. Through-a-node paths. Diameter (543), Max Path Sum (124), Longest Univalue Path (687), Longest ZigZag (1372), Binary Tree Cameras (968): return the one-sided value to the parent, update the two-sided answer locally. Re-read chapter 41 if this is not immediate.
  6. Leaf-to-leaf paths. Number of Good Leaf Nodes Pairs (1530) and Smallest Subtree with all the Deepest Nodes (865) require combining information from both children at the parent — a postorder return of a collection, not a scalar.
  7. Path with a string accumulator. Binary Tree Paths (257) joins with '->'; Smallest String Starting From Leaf (988) builds the string bottom-up and must reverse it (or build a list of characters and reverse at the leaf).
  8. Pseudo-palindromic paths (1457) carries a bitmask of odd-count digits down the path; a path is pseudo-palindromic iff the mask has at most one set bit (mask & (mask - 1) == 0). That one-line test is worth memorising — it is the standard ‘at most one odd’ check.
  9. Distribute Coins (979) returns node.val - 1 + left_excess + right_excess and adds abs(...) of each child’s return to the move count. The return value is ‘net coins this subtree needs to send up’.
  10. If the problem says ‘path’ and does not say ‘root to leaf’, assume it means any downward path and reach for the hybrid template.

Tree – LCA, Structure, and Serialization

The Kernel

Three sub-families that all reduce to ‘compare two trees’ or ‘encode a tree uniquely’. LCA is a postorder search; serialization is a preorder with explicit nulls.

38
Problems mapped
4
Easy
31
Medium

The Boundary Rules

  1. LCA in a binary tree (236). Postorder: if node is None, or node is p, or node is q, return node. Otherwise recurse both sides. If both returns are non-null, the current node is the LCA; otherwise return whichever side was non-null. This is the single most elegant five-line algorithm in the tree part — memorise it verbatim.
  2. LCA in a BST (235) is the bound walk from chapter 42, not the postorder search. Using the general algorithm on a BST is correct but wastes the ordering and will be flagged.
  3. LCA with parent pointers (1650) is the intersection of two linked lists — use the two-pointer wraparound from chapter 35, or a visited set.
  4. Serialization (297). Preorder with an explicit '#' for nulls is the standard. Deserialization uses an iterator over the tokens and consumes one per call — next(it) inside the recursion. Do not pass an index around; the iterator makes the code half as long.
  5. Delimiter choice matters: with multi-digit values, '1' + '2' and '12' collide unless you join with a separator such as ','. Always state the separator.
  6. Duplicate subtrees (652). Serialize each subtree bottom-up and hash it into a Counter. The key can be the serialized string or a tuple of (val, left_id, right_id) with an id-map for O(1) keys. The id-map version is O(n) and is the better answer; the string version is easier to explain.
  7. Verify preorder serialization (331) is a slot-counting problem, not a tree-building problem: start with 1 slot, each node consumes one and adds two, each '#' consumes one and adds zero; the sequence is valid iff the count never goes negative and ends at zero.
  8. Construct from traversals (105, 106, 889) belongs here too — the preorder/inorder split is the same ‘find the root, split the rest’ idea that serialization relies on.
  9. Flip equivalent (951) is Same Tree with an extra recursive case that tries the unflipped children. Two extra lines.
  10. Symmetric (101) is Same Tree with mirrored recursion, and Subtree (572) is Same Tree nested inside a traversal. Once you have Same Tree you have all three.

Part X · Backtracking
Chapter 45

Backtracking – The Universal Template

The Kernel

Choose, recurse, un-choose. Every backtracking problem in this book is that three-step loop; the only differences are what a ‘choice’ is, how you iterate the choices, and what makes a partial solution invalid.

35
Problems mapped
2
Easy
32
Medium
1
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The template. def bt(start, path): if <goal>: result.append(path.copy()); return; for i in <choices from start>: if <invalid>: continue; path.append(choice); bt(i + 1, path); path.pop().
  2. path.copy() on every result append. Appending path itself makes every answer alias the same list. This is the number-one backtracking bug in every language.
  3. path.pop() must run even on the continue path. Use continue (not return) for pruning, and never return from inside the loop unless the choices are sorted and you are pruning the rest — in which case say why.
  4. The three axis questions. (1) Is the choice set the remaining elements (combinations) or all elements (permutations)? (2) Can an element be reused? (3) Do duplicate answers need removing? The answers determine the loop bound and the dedup rule, and nothing else changes.
  5. Combinations loop from start. for i in range(start, n). This enforces non-decreasing index order and prevents [1,2] and [2,1] both appearing.
  6. Permutations loop from 0 with a used array. for i in range(n): if used[i]: continue. The used array is what stops an element being picked twice.
  7. Reuse allowed -> recurse with i; reuse forbidden -> recurse with i + 1. That single character is the difference between Combination Sum (39) and Combination Sum II (40).
  8. The dedup rule. Sort the input first, then skip if i > start and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue. Note it is i > start, not i > 0 — at the top of a level you must be allowed to pick the first duplicate.
  9. Prune with sorting. If the choices are sorted, if a[i] > remaining: break replaces continue and prunes the whole suffix. Always sort when the problem permits it.
  10. Complexity. Subsets and combinations are O(2^n); permutations are O(n!); grid search with a path length L is O(m n 4^L). State the bound — backtracking is only acceptable when the input is small, and saying why is part of the answer.
  11. When to stop backtracking and use DP instead. If the question asks for a count or an optimum rather than an enumeration, and the subproblems overlap, it is DP. Target Sum (494) and Combination Sum IV (377) both have backtracking statements and DP answers; only 377 genuinely needs DP for the counting version.

Chapter 46

Backtracking – Subsets and Combinations

The Kernel

Subsets is the ‘include or exclude’ binary tree; combinations is subsets with a fixed size. Both are the start-index loop with no invalid state to check.

26
Problems mapped
2
Easy
24
Medium
0
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Subsets (78): record the path at every node, not just at leaves. The number of answers is 2^n, and each corresponds to a node in the recursion tree.
  2. There are two equivalent formulations: the index loop (for i in range(start, n)) and the include/exclude pair (bt(i+1, path + [a[i]]) / bt(i+1, path)). The index loop is more efficient because it avoids copying; the include/exclude form is easier to prove correct. Prefer the index loop.
  3. Subsets II (90) adds duplicates: sort, then if i > start and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue. That is the entire change.
  4. Combinations (77) adds a size limit: if len(path) == k: result.append(path.copy()); return.
  5. Prune combinations with an arithmetic bound. In range(start, n) you only need range(start, n - (k - len(path)) + 1) — there is no point starting so late that you cannot reach k elements. This is a genuine optimisation that interviewers reward.
  6. Combination Sum III (216) fixes both the size (k) and the sum (n) over digits 1-9. The pruning is if remaining < 0: break.
  7. Letter Combinations of a Phone Number (17) is a Cartesian product, not a subset problem: the loop is over the digits, and the choice set per digit is fixed by a lookup table. Same template, different choices.
  8. Generate Parentheses (22) is a constrained construction: track open_count and close_count and only recurse when open < n or close < open. The constraint is the pruning, and it produces exactly the Catalan number of valid strings with no post-filter.
  9. Factor Combinations (254) loops from the last factor onward (range(start, isqrt(n) + 1)) and pushes a copy of the path at every step where the remainder is 1. The isqrt bound avoids duplicate factorisations.
  10. Letter Case Permutation (784) branches on each character: digits have one branch, letters have two. path + [c.swapcase()] is the second branch.
  11. Count of Maximum OR subsets (2044) is a subset enumeration with an aggregate — no path list at all, just a running OR and a count. Recognise when the ‘path’ can be reduced to a scalar.

Part X · Backtracking
Chapter 47

Backtracking – Permutations and the Dedup Rule

The Kernel

Permutations loop over all indices with a used mask, because order matters. The dedup rule changes from ‘compare with the previous index’ to ‘compare with the previous unused index’.

17
Problems mapped
0
Easy
14
Medium
3
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Permutations (46): for i in range(n): if used[i]: continue; used[i] = True; path.append(a[i]); bt(); path.pop(); used[i] = False. Un-choose the mask as well as the path — forgetting the mask reset is a silent wrong answer.
  2. Permutations II (47) dedup rule: sort, then if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i-1] and not used[i-1]: continue. The not used[i-1] clause is the crucial part: it means 'this duplicate’s predecessor is not currently in use, so we are at the top of a level and must take the first duplicate only'.
  3. Why not used[i-1] and not used[i-1]? Because if the previous duplicate is in use, we are extending a path that already contains it, and that is a legitimate distinct permutation. Get this backwards and you silently drop valid answers. This is the single most subtle line in the backtracking part.
  4. Swap-based permutations are the O(1)-extra-space alternative: swap a[i] with a[start], recurse, swap back. But the swap version cannot dedup easily (the array is not sorted after swapping), so for 47 the used-mask version is strictly better.
  5. Next Permutation (31) is not backtracking at all — it is a three-step in-place algorithm: find the longest non-increasing suffix, swap the pivot with the smallest larger element in the suffix, then reverse the suffix. Memorise it; it is asked constantly.
  6. Permutation Sequence (60) needs the kth permutation without enumerating: use the factorial number system. k // (n-1)! picks the index from the remaining sorted digits. This is O(n^2) and is the answer to ‘can you do better than enumerating?’. 31 plus k-1 iterations is the fallback.
  7. Non-decreasing Subsequences (491) is a subset problem whose dedup cannot use sorting (the order must be preserved). The fix is a per-level set of values already tried at this depth. Recognise that when sorting is forbidden, the dedup mechanism must change.
  8. Letter Tile Possibilities (1079) is ‘count all permutations of all subsets’ — a Counter plus recursion over the distinct letters. The Counter replaces the used array and handles duplicates for free.
  9. Beautiful Arrangement (526) and Count Arrangement problems are permutation enumeration with a divisibility predicate; the pruning is if (i+1) % pos == 0 or pos % (i+1) == 0.

Backtracking – Target Sum and Partitioning

The Kernel

Same template, but the pruning is arithmetic: sort the choices and break as soon as the remaining target goes negative. The problem becomes a search over a constrained sum.

24
Problems mapped
0
Easy
21
Medium
3
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Combination Sum (39): reuse allowed, so recurse with i (not i + 1). Prune with if a[i] > remaining: break after sorting.
  2. Combination Sum II (40): each element used once, so recurse with i + 1; add the dedup line. Two changes from 39, both one character.
  3. The sort-and-break rule. Sorting is what converts continue into break and gives you real pruning. Without sorting, Combination Sum is still correct but exponentially slower on adversarial inputs.
  4. Target Sum (494) has a backtracking solution (+ or - for each element) and a DP solution. The DP reduction is the important part: sum(P) - sum(N) = target and sum(P) + sum(N) = total, so sum(P) = (target + total) / 2. If (target + total) is odd or negative, the answer is zero. The problem then becomes 'count subsets summing to (target+total)/2' — a 0/1 knapsack count. That reduction is the interview.
  5. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) is the hardest member. Two accelerations matter: (1) sort descending and put the largest elements first, because they are the most constrained; (2) skip a bucket if it is empty and the element failed there (if bucket[j] == 0: break). Without both, the exponential blow-up times out.
  6. Matchsticks to Square (473) is 698 with k = 4. Same code, smaller constant.
  7. Palindrome Partitioning (131) is a partition search where the validity check is s[i:j+1] == s[i:j+1][::-1]. Precomputing a palindrome table with DP turns the check from O(n) to O(1) and is the expected optimisation.
  8. Restore IP Addresses (93) is 131 with a different validity check (each segment 0-255, no leading zeros) and exactly four segments. The ‘exactly four’ constraint means you prune on the segment count.
  9. Expression Add Operators (282) is the hardest: the choices are + - at every split, and multiplication needs a prev_operand to undo precedence correctly. The trick is to carry the last operand and pass cur - prev + prev val on a *. If you cannot derive it, at least state the precedence problem out loud.
  10. Word Break II (140) is a backtracking over a dictionary plus memoisation on the suffix — otherwise it is exponential. Recognise when backtracking needs a memo to survive the constraints.
  11. 24 Game (679) is a backtracking over pairwise reductions: pick two numbers, apply an operator, recurse on the reduced list. The choice space is not ‘elements’ but ‘pairs’, which is a different loop shape.

Chapter 49

Backtracking – Grid Search

The Kernel

The choice set is the four neighbours. Mark the cell before recursing and unmark it after — that is grid backtracking, and it is DFS with a restore step.

20
Problems mapped
0
Easy
13
Medium
7
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The four-neighbour loop. for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)). Define it once at the top of the function; writing four explicit recursive calls is error-prone.
  2. Mark and unmark. grid[r][c] = '#' before the recursion, grid[r][c] = original after. This is the grid version of path.pop(). Forgetting the restore means the first path wins and every other path is blocked.
  3. Word Search (79): match the character, mark, recurse on the four neighbours with index + 1, unmark. The bounds check 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C must come before the character comparison.
  4. Word Search II (212) is 79 repeated for every word, which is O(words cells 4^L). The correct answer is a Trie plus one DFS: build a Trie of all words, then do a single grid DFS that walks the Trie in lockstep. When a Trie node is terminal, record the word. Prune by removing matched words from the Trie. This is the single best example in the book of a data structure eliminating a nested loop.
  5. Unique Paths III (980) must visit every non-obstacle cell exactly once, so the goal test is steps == total_non_obstacle and not just ‘reached the end’. Counting the target cells first is required.
  6. Path with Maximum Gold (1219) is mark/unmark with a value accumulator and a best update. It never needs to reach a specific cell.
  7. Flood-fill problems that do NOT need unmarking. Number of Islands (200), Max Area of Island (695), Surrounded Regions (130) are connected component problems: once a cell is visited it belongs to the component forever, so there is no restore. The distinction is whether the question is about a path (restore) or a region (do not restore). That is the key discrimination in this chapter.
  8. Surrounded Regions (130) has a beautiful trick: instead of finding surrounded regions, find the unsurrounded ones by flooding inward from the border, then flip everything untouched. Recognising the complement is the whole problem.
  9. Pacific Atlantic Water Flow (417) is the same complement trick: flood uphill from both oceans' borders and intersect the reachable sets. Doing it forward from every cell is O((mn)^2); doing it backward from the borders is O(mn).
  10. Sudoku Solver (37) and N-Queens (51) are grid backtracking with row/column/box constraint sets. For 37, three sets of frozenset/bitmasks (rows, cols, boxes) make the validity check O(1); scanning the grid each time is 27x slower and is the usual reason a solution times out.

Chapter 50

Backtracking – Constraint Satisfaction

The Kernel

The choices are constrained by everything already placed. The engineering is in making the validity check O(1) with auxiliary sets, and in choosing the most-constrained variable first.

22
Problems mapped
1
Easy
10
Medium
11
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. N-Queens (51): the constraint is not just ‘same column’ but two diagonals. Track three sets: cols, diag1 (where r - c is constant), diag2 (where r + c is constant). Adding and removing from three sets is O(1); scanning the board is O(n).
  2. The diagonal encoding is the insight: two cells are on the same \ diagonal iff r - c is equal, and on the same / diagonal iff r + c is equal. Memorise both.
  3. N-Queens II (52) is 51 with a counter instead of a board — same code, drop the construction.
  4. Sudoku Solver (37): three arrays of 9 bitmasks (or sets) for rows, columns and 3x3 boxes. The box index is (r // 3) * 3 + (c // 3). Bitmask arithmetic (mask & (1 << d)) is fastest; sets are more readable. Choose based on how the interviewer reacts.
  5. Most-constrained-variable heuristic. In Sudoku and similar CSPs, choosing the empty cell with the fewest legal values first prunes dramatically. You do not need it to pass LeetCode, but mentioning it is the difference between a good and an excellent answer.
  6. Valid Sudoku (36) is the checking version with no backtracking — one pass with the same three mask arrays. Do not over-engineer it.
  7. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) is a CSP: the variables are elements, the constraints are bucket capacities. Sorting descending and breaking on an empty bucket that already failed are the two heuristics that make it pass.
  8. Matchsticks to Square (473) is 698 with k = 4 and a divisibility pre-check (sum % 4 != 0 -> impossible).
  9. Verbal arithmetic (1307), cryptarithm (2850-ish) and Maximum Number of Achievable Transfer Requests (1601) are constraint problems where the search space must be reduced by an algebraic observation before backtracking becomes viable. 1601 reduces to ‘subset of requests whose net degree change is all zero’.
  10. The universal CSP checklist to say out loud: (1) what are the variables, (2) what is the domain of each, (3) what are the constraints, (4) which variable is most constrained, (5) can any constraint be encoded as O(1) state.

Chapter 51

Grid Flood Fill – The Islands Family

The Kernel

A grid is an implicit graph: each cell is a node, each of its four neighbours is an edge. ‘Connected component’ questions are then a plain DFS/BFS with a visited marker — and there is no unmarking.

34
Problems mapped
2
Easy
26
Medium
6
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Mark on entry, not on push. grid[r][c] = '0' at the top of the DFS prevents both infinite recursion and duplicate work. Marking on push works for BFS but not for DFS — pick ‘mark on entry’ and use it for both.
  2. In-place marking vs a visited set. For 0/1 grids, mutating the grid is O(1) extra space and is the preferred answer. Mention that you are mutating the input and offer to restore it if the caller needs the original.
  3. Islands family, one template: Number of Islands (200) counts components; Max Area of Island (695) returns the largest component size; Island Perimeter (463) adds 4 per cell and subtracts 2 per shared edge; Number of Closed Islands (1254) excludes components that touch the border; Number of Enclaves (1020) counts the cells in non-border components; Count Sub Islands (1905) counts islands in grid2 fully contained in an island of grid1.
  4. Flood Fill (733) is the same traversal with a colour change — the warm-up version of this chapter.
  5. The complement trick. Surrounded Regions (130) floods from the border inward to find the escaping cells, then flips everything else. Pacific Atlantic (417) floods uphill from both ocean borders and intersects. Both avoid the O((mn)^2) forward search. Whenever a problem asks about cells that can reach a boundary, search from the boundary.
  6. Making A Large Island (827) requires labelling each island with an id and recording its size, then, for each 0 cell, summing the distinct neighbour ids. The distinctness check is essential — two neighbours can belong to the same island and would be double counted.
  7. Number of Provinces (547) is the adjacency-matrix version of 200. The same DFS works, but Union-Find (chapter 55) is usually cleaner.
  8. Boundary checks. Write a helper in_bounds(r, c) once. Inlining four comparisons in four places is how index bugs get in.
  9. Iterative vs recursive DFS. A 300x300 grid can have a 90,000-deep recursion path in the worst case (a spiral), which exceeds Python’s default limit. Use an explicit stack for grid DFS, or raise the limit. This is a real failure mode, not a theoretical one.
  10. Multi-source BFS vs DFS. DFS answers ‘what is connected’; BFS answers ‘how far’. If the question contains ‘nearest’, ‘minimum steps’, or ‘distance’, it is chapter 52, not this one.

Chapter 52

Graph BFS – Unweighted Shortest Path

The Kernel

BFS explores in rings of increasing distance, so the first time you reach a node you have reached it by a shortest path. That is the entire justification for using BFS instead of DFS here.

38
Problems mapped
0
Easy
27
Medium
11
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Mark visited when you enqueue, not when you dequeue. Marking on dequeue lets the same node enter the queue multiple times and can blow up the frontier exponentially. This is the most common BFS performance bug.
  2. Track distance in the queue, either by storing (node, dist) tuples or by the level-size idiom (for _ in range(len(q)):) with an outer counter. The level-size idiom is more memory-efficient; the tuple is easier to get right.
  3. Early exit. Return as soon as you pop or enqueue the target — there is no need to finish the level, because BFS guarantees the first arrival is optimal. Word Ladder (127) is the classic case where failing to exit early is the difference between passing and timing out.
  4. Building the adjacency list. defaultdict(list), then one pass over the edge list. For an undirected graph add both directions — forgetting the reverse edge is the most common graph bug in existence.
  5. Implicit graphs. Word Ladder (127) has edges between words differing by one character — generating neighbours is O(26 L) with wildcard bucketing (ht -> [hot, hit]) or O(n * L) by pairwise comparison. The wildcard bucket is the optimisation that makes it pass.
  6. Open the Lock (752) and Minimum Genetic Mutation (433) are the same implicit-graph BFS with a small alphabet. Recognise the family: state space + allowed moves + fewest moves.
  7. Bidirectional BFS halves the branching factor: expand from both ends and stop when the frontiers intersect. Word Ladder is the canonical use case. It is O(b^(d/2)) instead of O(b^d). Mention it as an optimisation; implement it only if asked.
  8. Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination (1293) adds a resource to the state: the visited set becomes (r, c, k_remaining), and a cell can be revisited with a larger remaining budget. Recognise when the visited key must include extra state.
  9. Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes (847) is BFS over (node, visited_bitmask) — the state is a bitmask, and the answer is the first state where the mask is full. This is the bridge between BFS and bitmask DP (chapter 79).
  10. Bus Routes (815) is BFS over routes rather than stops — the insight is that the nodes of your BFS graph need not be the entities in the problem statement.
  11. Snakes and Ladders (909) is a flat BFS over squares with a coordinate conversion. Minimum Knight Moves (1197) is a flat BFS over a board with eight moves and a symmetry optimisation.
  12. If all edges have the same weight, BFS is optimal. If weights differ, you need Dijkstra (chapter 56) or 0-1 BFS (chapter 53). Saying this sentence in an interview signals that you know why BFS works.

Chapter 53

Multi-Source BFS and 0-1 BFS

The Kernel

Seed the queue with all the starting points at once, and every cell gets the distance to its nearest source in one pass. For edge weights in {0, 1}, use a deque and push 0-weight edges to the front.

16
Problems mapped
0
Easy
13
Medium
3
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Multi-source template. q = deque(all_sources); then a plain BFS. The only change from chapter 52 is the initialisation. But the payoff is huge: it turns ‘for each cell, find the nearest source’ from O(mn * s) into O(mn).
  2. Rotting Oranges (994) seeds with every rotten orange and counts levels; the answer is the number of levels until the queue empties, and you must check that no fresh orange remains. Forgetting that check is the classic wrong answer.
  3. 01 Matrix (542) seeds with every 0 and BFSs outward. The DP alternative (two passes, one from the top-left and one from the bottom-right) is O(mn) with no queue and is worth knowing as a cross-check.
  4. As Far from Land as Possible (1162) is 542 plus a maximum over the distances. Walls and Gates (286) is the same problem with a different sentinel.
  5. 0-1 BFS. When edges have weight 0 or 1, a deque replaces the priority queue: appendleft for weight-0 edges and append for weight-1 edges. The deque stays sorted by distance, so it is O(V + E) instead of Dijkstra’s O(E log V).
  6. The 0-1 BFS correctness argument: at any moment the deque contains at most two distinct distances, d and d + 1, and both pushes preserve that. State this if asked why a deque suffices.
  7. When a node is finalised in 0-1 BFS, you may need a visited check on pop because a node can be pushed twice with different distances. Pop-and-skip-if-visited is the standard guard.
  8. Multi-source + grid is also the right frame for Shortest Bridge (934) (label one island, then multi-source BFS to the other) and Minimum Knight Moves with several targets.
  9. Do not use multi-source BFS when the sources have different costs. Different starting costs require a priority queue (Dijkstra with all sources pushed at their own initial distance).
  10. Nearest Exit from Entrance in a Maze (1926) is a single-source BFS with a border test instead of a target — recognise that ‘reaches the boundary’ is a goal condition.

Chapter 54

Topological Sort

The Kernel

Ordering with prerequisites is a DAG. Kahn’s algorithm is BFS on in-degrees; the DFS version is postorder reversed. If a cycle exists, the topological order is incomplete — and that incompleteness is usually the actual answer.

25
Problems mapped
3
Easy
12
Medium
10
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Kahn’s algorithm. Build indegree[] and the adjacency list; seed the queue with every node of in-degree 0; pop, append to the order, and decrement each neighbour’s in-degree, enqueuing at zero. If the final order is shorter than the node count, there is a cycle. That check is the answer to Course Schedule (207).
  2. The indegree construction is where the bugs live. For each edge (u, v): adj[u].append(v); indegree[v] += 1. Getting the direction backwards produces a reversed order that still looks plausible.
  3. DFS version. Postorder DFS, appending a node after its descendants, then reverse the result. Cycle detection needs a three-colour state: white (unvisited), grey (on the stack), black (done). A grey neighbour means a cycle. The three colours are mandatory — a plain visited set cannot distinguish ‘on the current path’ from ‘finished’.
  4. Course Schedule (207) asks ‘is there a cycle’; Course Schedule II (210) asks for the order. One algorithm, different return value.
  5. Alien Dictionary (269) is topological sort where you must first derive the edges by comparing adjacent words. Two edge cases decide correctness: a prefix word placed after a longer word is invalid, and fewer than k distinct letters means you must append the missing ones in arbitrary order.
  6. Minimum Height Trees (310) is reverse Kahn: repeatedly peel leaves; the last one or two nodes remaining are the roots. The insight that MHT roots are the tree’s centroids is what makes it O(n) instead of O(n^2).
  7. Find Eventual Safe States (802) is reverse topological sort — work backwards from the terminal nodes. Or colour-DFS forward. Both are accepted; the reverse Kahn version is more elegant.
  8. Sort Items by Groups (1203) is two-level topological sort: once over the groups and once within each group, then merge. It is the hardest problem in this chapter.
  9. Sequence Reconstruction (444) and Parallel Courses (1136) are direct applications. 444 adds a uniqueness requirement: the order is reconstructible iff the queue never holds more than one node at a time.
  10. When to reach for topological sort. Any problem with ‘prerequisite’, ‘before’, ‘dependency’, ‘order’, or ‘can be finished’ language, plus any DAG reachability question.

Chapter 55

Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)

The Kernel

Two operations: find(x) returns a representative; union(a, b) merges two sets. With path compression and union by size it is effectively O(1) per operation, and it answers connectivity questions incrementally.

42
Problems mapped
0
Easy
24
Medium
18
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The implementation, memorised. parent = list(range(n)), size = [1] * n; find with path halving (while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]); union by attaching the smaller root to the larger and updating size.
  2. Both optimisations matter. Path compression alone gives O(log n) amortised; union by size alone gives O(log n); together they give O(alpha(n)), which is effectively constant. Interviewers expect both.
  3. Use Union-Find when the edges arrive incrementally, or when the question is ‘are these connected’, or when you need to count components after a sequence of merges. Use DFS/BFS when you have the whole graph and one connectivity question.
  4. Redundant Connection (684): process edges one at a time; the first edge whose endpoints are already in the same set is the redundant one. This is Union-Find’s canonical use — an incremental cycle test.
  5. Redundant Connection II (685) is the directed version and is much harder: handle the two cases (a node with in-degree 2, or a cycle). The in-degree-2 check comes first, and if both exist the answer is the edge that both creates the cycle and is a second parent.
  6. Accounts Merge (721)**: union the emails within each account, then group by root and sort. The find-as-dict-key step is the pattern.
  7. Satisfiability of Equality Equations (990): union all == first, then check that no != has both sides in the same set. Order matters — two passes, not one.
  8. Number of Provinces (547) and Number of Connected Components (323): count roots by sum(1 for i in range(n) if find(i) == i). Remember to find first — a node whose parent chain was compressed lazily may not point at the root directly.
  9. Largest Component Size by Common Factor (952): union each number with its prime factors, using the primes as pseudo-nodes. The reduction from ‘shared factor’ to ‘shared prime’ is the insight.
  10. Min Cost to Connect All Points (1584) is Kruskal’s MST: sort all edges by weight and union greedily, skipping edges whose endpoints are already connected. Union-Find is the engine; the greedy is the algorithm.
  11. Couples Holding Hands (765) is a counting problem solvable by Union-Find or by a greedy swap pass. The Union-Find version counts components and answers n - components.
  12. Union-Find cannot un-merge. If the problem needs deletion, you need a different structure (offline reverse processing, or a dynamic connectivity structure). Recognising this limitation is itself worth saying.

Chapter 56

Weighted Shortest Path – Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd

The Kernel

Three algorithms, three conditions. All weights non-negative -> Dijkstra. Negative weights allowed -> Bellman-Ford. All-pairs with small n -> Floyd-Warshall.

34
Problems mapped
0
Easy
20
Medium
14
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Dijkstra, memorised. dist = {src: 0}; a min-heap of (distance, node) seeded with (0, src); pop; if the popped distance exceeds the stored distance, skip (lazy deletion); relax each edge and push improved distances. The lazy-deletion skip is what makes the visited set unnecessary and keeps the code short.
  2. Dijkstra fails on negative edges. It is greedy: once a node is finalised it is never revisited. State this limitation before using it — it is a standard interview question.
  3. Complexity is O(E log V). Say it out loud.
  4. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V - 1 times. O(VE). Use it when edges can be negative, or when the number of hops is limited — Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (787) is Bellman-Ford with exactly K + 1 relaxation rounds, and each round must use a copy* of the previous distance array so a single round cannot chain. Forgetting the copy is the classic bug.
  5. Network Delay Time (743) is textbook Dijkstra: run from the source and take the maximum finalised distance. If any node is unreachable, return -1.
  6. Path With Minimum Effort (1631) and Swim in Rising Water (778) are Dijkstra on a grid where the ‘distance’ is a running maximum rather than a sum. The relaxation becomes new = max(d, |height diff|) or new = max(d, grid[nr][nc]). Recognising that Dijkstra works for any monotone combination, not just sums, is the transferable insight.
  7. Path with Maximum Probability (1514) is Dijkstra with a max-heap on probabilities — the same algorithm with the comparison flipped. Dijkstra works on any order-preserving semiring.
  8. Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination (1976) adds a counting array alongside dist: when a shorter path is found, reset the count; when an equal path is found, add to it. This is the standard ‘shortest-path counting’ extension.
  9. Floyd-Warshall is three nested loops with k outermost — dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). The k loop must be outermost; swapping the order gives a wrong answer. O(V^3), so only for V <= 400.
  10. Evaluate Division (399) is a graph problem in disguise: a / b = 2 is a weighted edge. Build the graph, then DFS or Floyd-Warshall over ratios. Recognising the graph structure is the whole problem.
  11. Path with Maximum Minimum Value (1102) is the grid version of 778 and is also solvable by Union-Find with descending edge weights — know both.
  12. Choosing the algorithm in an interview. Say: 'all weights are non-negative, so Dijkstra; if hops are limited I need Bellman-Ford; if I needed all pairs with n under 400, Floyd-Warshall.' That one sentence covers the whole chapter.

Bipartite Graphs and Colouring

The Kernel

Two-colour the graph by BFS/DFS. If you ever need a third colour, the graph is not bipartite. The colour array doubles as the visited set.

13
Problems mapped
0
Easy
6
Medium
7
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The two-colour BFS. color = [-1] * n; for each uncoloured node, colour it 0 and BFS, requiring every neighbour to be the opposite colour. A conflict means not bipartite.
  2. The colour array replaces visited. -1 means unvisited, 0 and 1 are the colours. Do not maintain a separate visited set — it is redundant and creates a second source of truth.
  3. Loop over all nodes. A graph can be disconnected; starting from node 0 only checks one component. The for i in range(n): if color[i] == -1 wrapper is mandatory.
  4. Odd cycles are exactly the obstruction. A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd-length cycle. Being able to say this is the conceptual answer interviewers want.
  5. Possible Bipartition (886) is Is Graph Bipartite (785) with the graph built from a ‘dislike’ list. The graph construction is the only new work.
  6. Is Graph Bipartite (785) is also Union-Find-solvable: for each edge, union the neighbours of each endpoint together; if an edge’s endpoints end up in the same set, it is not bipartite. That is a nice alternative to offer.
  7. Flower Planting With No Adjacent (1042) is greedy colouring, not 2-colouring: each node has at most 3 neighbours, so 4 colours always suffice and you can pick any colour not used by a neighbour. Do not confuse it with bipartiteness.
  8. K-colouring in general is NP-hard. Only 2-colouring is polynomial. Saying this stops you from attempting the wrong thing under pressure.
  9. Shortest Path with Alternating Colors (1129) is BFS where the state includes the colour of the last edge. The visited set becomes visited[node][color]. It is the same ‘extra state in the key’ idea as chapter 52’s 1293.
  10. Bipartite matching (Hungarian algorithm, Hopcroft-Karp) is beyond most interviews, but Maximum Students Taking Exam (1349) and Maximum Compatibility Score Sum (1947) are assignment problems that reduce to it. Know the name and the reduction.

Chapter 58

Matrix Manipulation – Rotate, Spiral, and In-Place Marks

The Kernel

Four index formulas cover every matrix problem: the transpose swap, the four-way rotation cycle, the spiral boundary shrink, and divmod for flattening.

63
Problems mapped
24
Easy
36
Medium
3
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Transpose is for i in range(n): for j in range(i+1, n): a[i][j], a[j][i] = a[j][i], a[i][j]. The i+1 start is what avoids double-swapping.
  2. Rotate 90 clockwise = transpose, then reverse each row. Rotate 90 counter-clockwise = transpose, then reverse the row order. Rotate 180 = reverse rows and reverse each row. Two operations, no index arithmetic — far safer than the four-way cycle swap.
  3. The four-way cycle (if you must do it in one pass): a[i][j] -> a[j][n-1-i] -> a[n-1-i][n-1-j] -> a[n-1-j][i] -> a[i][j]. The four cells involved are the corners of a rotating square; you only need to iterate i over the top-left quadrant.
  4. Spiral traversal (54) is four boundary pointers top, bottom, left, right that shrink after each side. The re-check before the third and fourth sides is mandatory — on a single-row or single-column remnant you will otherwise emit duplicates. if top <= bottom before the bottom row and if left <= right before the left column.
  5. Spiral generation (59) is the same four pointers writing instead of reading. Spiral Matrix III (885) is a different construction: walk in increasing step lengths, turning at the right moments.
  6. Set Matrix Zeroes (73) is the flagship in-place marking problem. The O(1)-space solution uses the first row and first column as the marker arrays, with two extra booleans for the first row/column themselves. You must process the first row and column last, or the markers overwrite data before it is read.
  7. Game of Life (289) is the same idea: encode the next state in a second bit of the existing cell (0b10 for ‘was alive, now dead’), then do a second pass shifting right. Using two bits instead of a copy is the expected answer.
  8. Search a 2D Matrix (74) flattens to 1-D with row, col = divmod(mid, n). Search a 2D Matrix II (240) is the top-right walk (chapter 10). Two problems, two completely different approaches — do not mix them up.
  9. Diagonal traversal (498) has two directions and a boundary flip. The if r == 0 / if c == 0 flip logic is fiddly; write it as ‘move up-right, and if you exit, re-enter at the correct edge’.
  10. Prefix-sum rectangles (304, 1314) belong to chapter 16; matrix DP (62, 64, 221) belongs to chapter 67. Recognise which of the three matrix families a problem belongs to before writing code.

Part XII

Dynamic Programming

Sixteen chapters. DP is recursion plus a cache; the state design is the skill, and the loop directions are the traps.

Part XII · Dynamic Programming
Chapter 59

DP – How to Think About It

The Kernel

DP is recursion plus a cache. If you can write the brute-force recursion and name its state, the DP is mechanical. Never start from the table — start from the recursion.

4
Problems mapped
1
Easy
3
Medium
0
Hard

The Method

  1. The 4-step method. (1) Write the brute-force recursion. (2) Identify the state — the arguments that fully determine the answer. (3) Add a cache keyed on the state. (4) Convert to a bottom-up table only if it saves memory or the interviewer asks. Steps 1-3 are what you should do in an interview.
  2. State design is the whole skill. The state must be (a) sufficient — it determines the future, and (b) minimal — it has no redundant components. If your state includes an index into the input and a derived quantity, the derived quantity is probably redundant.
  3. Two DP idioms, and you should pick one per problem. Take-it-or-leave-it (f(i) = best(f(i-1), value(i) + f(i-2))) for selection problems; try-every-choice (f(i) = best over j of g(f(j), cost(i,j))) for partition problems.
  4. The n + 1 sizing rule. Allocate tables of size n + 1 (or m + 1 x n + 1) and define dp[i] as 'the answer for the first i elements'. The extra row/column is the empty prefix, and it removes every if i == 0 branch from the loop body.
  5. Top-down vs bottom-up. Top-down is easier to write correctly and only computes reachable states. Bottom-up is faster in Python because it avoids function-call overhead, and it enables the rolling-array optimisation. Write top-down first to get it correct, then convert if you have time.
  6. Rolling arrays. If dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1] (and maybe dp[i-2]), you can reduce the table to two variables. This is the standard follow-up question. For 2-D tables, iterate in the direction that lets you overwrite safely — for 0/1 knapsack that means iterating the capacity backwards.
  7. Initialisation is where most DP answers die. For minimisation, initialise to inf; for maximisation, to -inf (or 0 if the empty selection is allowed); for counting, to 0 with dp[0] = 1. Getting the sentinel wrong produces plausible-looking wrong answers.
  8. Order of evaluation. Bottom-up loops must be ordered so that every cell is computed after its dependencies. For 1-D that is left to right; for interval DP it is by length; for tree DP it is postorder; for bitmask DP it is by increasing mask.
  9. Counting mod 1e9+7. When the problem says ‘modulo 10^9 + 7’, apply % MOD at every addition. Applying it only at the end overflows in other languages and is a habit interviewers check.
  10. The three-question triage. (1) Is the answer an optimum, a count, or a yes/no? (2) Does the state need one index, two indices, an interval, or a mask? (3) Is there a greedy that is provably correct? If yes to (3), skip the DP entirely — greedy is shorter and faster.
Part XII · Dynamic Programming
Chapter 60

DP – 1D Linear Recurrence

The Kernel

dp[i] depends on a constant number of previous entries. Two variables suffice. This is the largest DP family and the one most often asked as a warm-up.

55
Problems mapped
7
Easy
37
Medium
11
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Climbing Stairs (70), Fibonacci (509), Tribonacci (1137), Min Cost Climbing Stairs (746) are dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] with different base cases and different coefficients. Write the two-variable rolling version directly.
  2. House Robber (198) is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]). House Robber II (213) is 198 run twice — once excluding the first house and once excluding the last — because the array is a circle. House Robber III (337) is the tree version and belongs to chapter 70.
  3. Delete and Earn (740) is House Robber after a bucket transform: points[v] = v * count(v), then rob the bucket array. Recognising the transform is the whole problem.
  4. Decode Ways (91) is the flagship 1-D string DP. dp[i] = ways to decode the first i characters; transitions from dp[i-1] (single digit, if non-zero) and dp[i-2] (two digits, if in 10..26). Both guards must be checked, and '0' alone contributes nothing.
  5. Integer Break (343) is dp[i] = max over j of max(j, dp[j]) * max(i-j, dp[i-j]). The max(j, dp[j]) is the subtle part — sometimes not breaking is better.
  6. Perfect Squares (279)** is a coin-change problem in disguise: coins are the squares, the target is n. Do not invent a new DP.
  7. Coin Change (322) is dp[i] = min(dp[i - c] + 1) over all coins c <= i. It is the unbounded knapsack (chapter 65) and is the single most-asked DP problem in existence. Initialise dp = [inf] * (n+1) with dp[0] = 0; the answer is -1 if dp[n] is still inf.
  8. Counting problems with dp[0] = 1. Count Ways To Build Good Strings (2466) and Student Attendance Record II (552) both have dp[0] = 1 and add contributions. The dp[0] = 1 seed means ‘there is one way to do nothing’.
  9. State-machine 1-D DP. Student Attendance Record II (552) and Knight Dialer (935) have dp[i][state] with a small state dimension. When you need to remember ‘how many consecutive X’, that is a state dimension, not an index.
  10. N-th Tribonacci and similar are also the standard demonstration of matrix exponentiation for O(log n) — worth knowing as a follow-up, never as the first answer.
  11. The recognition signal: ‘how many ways’, ‘minimum cost’, or ‘maximum value’ over a sequence where each element is processed once and the choice depends on a bounded number of predecessors.

Chapter 61

DP – Kadane and the Maximum Subarray Family

The Kernel

Kadane’s algorithm is one line: cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur). It is the maximum-subarray DP, and every variant changes exactly one of those two max calls.

20
Problems mapped
1
Easy
14
Medium
5
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The invariant. cur is the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index. The max(x, cur + x) is the decision ‘start fresh or extend’. State that invariant and the algorithm is obvious.
  2. Maximum Subarray (53) is the base form. Maximum Product Subarray (152) needs two running values — cur_max and cur_min — because multiplying a negative by a negative flips the ordering. Forgetting cur_min is the classic 152 bug.
  3. Maximum Sum Circular Subarray (918) is max(kadane(a), total - min_kadane(a)), with one special case: if all values are negative, the circular answer is invalid (it would be the empty subarray) and you must return the plain Kadane result.
  4. Maximum Subarray Sum with One Deletion (1186) keeps two states: keep (no deletion used) and delete (deletion used). The transition is delete = max(delete + x, keep).
  5. Maximum Absolute Sum (1749) is max(max_kadane, -min_kadane).
  6. K-Concatenation Maximum Sum (1191) splits by k: k == 1 is plain Kadane; k >= 2 and total > 0 is the circular-style answer; otherwise it is Kadane on the doubled array.
  7. Longest Turbulent Subarray (978) and Maximum Length of a Concatenated String-style problems use Kadane’s shape with a boolean comparison instead of a sum.
  8. Kadane as a DP is the same as Kadane as a running maximum. Both derivations are correct; present whichever the interviewer seems to prefer. The DP framing generalises better.
  9. Divide and conquer Kadane. 53 has an O(n log n) divide-and-conquer solution (best in the left, best in the right, best crossing the middle) which is the same idea as chapter 85’s merge-sort-based counting. Know it as the answer to ‘can you solve it without DP?’.
  10. The recognition signal: ‘contiguous subarray’ plus ‘maximum’ or ‘minimum’. If the problem says subsequence instead, it is chapter 62.

Chapter 62

DP – Longest Increasing Subsequence and Friends

The Kernel

dp[i] = length of the best subsequence ending at i. The O(n^2) version is obvious; the O(n log n) version replaces the table with a tails array and a binary search.

27
Problems mapped
1
Easy
18
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. O(n^2) form. dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for j < i if a[j] < a[i]). Always start here — it is correct, and it generalises to every variant.
  2. O(n log n) form. tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each x, i = bisect_left(tails, x); if i == len(tails): append, else tails[i] = x. The answer is len(tails). The bisect_left versus bisect_right choice is what switches between strictly increasing and non-decreasing. For strictly increasing use bisect_left.
  3. The tails array is not the subsequence. You cannot reconstruct the LIS from tails without extra bookkeeping (a parent array plus positions). Do not claim otherwise.
  4. Strict vs non-strict. Longest Increasing Subsequence (300) is strict (bisect_left). Maximum Length of Pair Chain (646) is strict on the second coordinate. Russian Doll Envelopes (354) is strict on both dimensions, which requires sorting width ascending and height descending so that equal widths cannot chain — that sort trick is the entire difficulty of 354.
  5. Counting the number of LIS (673) needs the O(n^2) form plus a count[] array: when dp[j] + 1 > dp[i], reset count[i] = count[j]; when equal, add. The tails array cannot do this.
  6. Longest String Chain (1048) is LIS on a DAG of words, sorted by length. The ‘is a predecessor’ test is a single deletion check.
  7. Longest Arithmetic Subsequence (1027) and its ‘given difference’ variant (1218) have dp[i][diff] as the state — a second dimension keyed on the difference. When the transition depends on a value rather than an index, the state gains a dimension keyed by that value.
  8. Length of Longest Fibonacci Subsequence (873) is the same value-keyed state: dp[i][j] = length of the Fibonacci-like sequence ending with a[i], a[j], and you look up a[j] - a[i] in a dict.
  9. Minimum Number of Removals to Make Mountain Array (1671) is LIS from the left plus LIS from the right, combined. Two passes, one answer.
  10. Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids (1691) is Russian Doll in 3-D after sorting each cuboid’s dimensions.
  11. Longest Increasing Subsequence is the parent of all ‘best subsequence with a local comparison’ problems. If the transition condition is a[j] < a[i] (or any pairwise predicate), the shape is LIS.

Chapter 63

DP – Two-Sequence DP (LCS and Edit Distance)

The Kernel

dp[i][j] = the answer using the first i characters of A and the first j characters of B. Two nested loops, three transitions: match, skip-A, skip-B. Every two-string DP in this book is this table.

19
Problems mapped
1
Easy
10
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The table is (m+1) x (n+1). The extra row and column are the empty prefixes, so dp[0][j] and dp[i][0] are the base cases and the loop body needs no special-casing.
  2. LCS (1143): if a[i-1] == b[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Note the i-1/j-1 indices inside the loop — the table is offset by one from the strings, and forgetting the offset is the most common bug.
  3. Edit Distance (72): if equal: dp[i-1][j-1] else 1 + min(dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The three terms are replace, delete, insert. Be able to name which is which — that is the standard follow-up question.
  4. The three-term structure is universal. Once you see dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], you can derive: Delete Operation for Two Strings (583) = m + n - 2 * LCS; Minimum ASCII Delete Sum (712) = edit distance with character values as costs; Uncrossed Lines (1035) = LCS exactly; Shortest Common Supersequence (1092) = m + n - LCS and the string is reconstructed by walking the table backwards.
  5. Wildcard Matching (44) and Regular Expression Matching (10) are two-sequence DP with a that matches any run. 44 has a one-dimensional greedy solution (two pointers with a backtrack point); 10 does not, because applies to the preceding element. Recognise the difference.
  6. Interleaving String (97) is dp[i][j] = 'the first i of A and j of B interleave to form the first i+j of C'. Two transitions, no min/max. The state is defined by the two indices, and i + j is implicit — if you ever find yourself writing dp[i][j][k], check whether k is derivable from i and j.
  7. Distinct Subsequences (115) counts, so the transition is + not max: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] plus dp[i-1][j-1] if the characters match.
  8. Rolling arrays. Every table in this chapter can be reduced to two rows, or even one row if you keep the dp[i-1][j-1] value in a temporary before overwriting. For edit distance, the one-row version needs a prev_diag variable — write it carefully.
  9. Reconstructing the answer. To output the actual LCS or the actual edit script, walk backwards from dp[m][n]: if the characters match and the value is consistent, take the diagonal; otherwise move to the cell that produced the value. Always check which predecessor was used — guessing the direction produces wrong strings.
  10. Longest Palindromic Subsequence (516) is LCS of the string with its reverse. That reduction converts a 1-D interval problem into this table, and it is worth knowing both framings.
  11. Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray (718) is LCS with contiguous matching: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 on match, 0 otherwise, and the answer is the table maximum (not dp[m][n]). Note that difference — contiguous means you reset on mismatch.

Chapter 64

DP – 0/1 Knapsack

The Kernel

dp[i][c] = the best value using the first i items with capacity c. Each item is either taken or not. The one-dimensional version iterates capacity backwards, and that direction is the whole difference from unbounded knapsack.

29
Problems mapped
1
Easy
18
Medium
10
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The 2-D recurrence. dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c - w[i]] + v[i]) for c >= w[i]. The i-1 in the second term is what makes each item usable once.
  2. The 1-D rolling version. for i: for c in range(C, w[i]-1, -1): dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]). Capacity iterates descending. Ascending would let item i be used multiple times, silently converting 0/1 knapsack into unbounded knapsack. This is the single most important line in the DP part.
  3. The mnemonic. Descending = each item once (0/1). Ascending = each item unlimited (unbounded). Same code, opposite loop direction, completely different problem.
  4. Partition Equal Subset Sum (416) is 0/1 knapsack with value == weight and target = total // 2. The pre-check if total % 2: return False is required.
  5. Target Sum (494) is 416 after the algebraic reduction from chapter 48: the target subset sum is (target + total) // 2.
  6. Last Stone Weight II (1049) is 416 phrased as ‘minimise the difference’, which is the same as 'maximise a subset sum under total/2'. Recognising the reduction is the problem.
  7. Ones and Zeroes (474) is 2-D 0/1 knapsack — the capacity is a pair (zeros, ones), so the DP table has two capacity dimensions and both must iterate descending. Getting one direction wrong is a classic error on this problem.
  8. Profitable Schemes (879) is knapsack where the ‘value’ dimension is clamped at the minimum required — profits above minProfit are equivalent, so the state is min(profit, minProfit). Clamping the value dimension is the trick.
  9. Counting rather than maximising. Replace max with +. Target Sum counts, Partition Equal Subset Sum decides, Last Stone Weight II minimises. The recurrence skeleton is identical.
  10. Profitable Schemes and Number of Ways to Form a Target String (1639) require % MOD at every addition.
  11. Boolean knapsack (416, Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets) can use a bitset instead of a list of booleans: dp |= dp << w. In Python that is one line and is dramatically faster. Offer it as an optimisation.
  12. The recognition signal. ‘Choose a subset’, ‘each item once’, ‘capacity or budget’, ‘maximise value / minimise difference / count ways’. If items can be reused, it is chapter 65.

Chapter 65

DP – Unbounded Knapsack and Coin Change

The Kernel

Items can be reused. Capacity iterates ascending, and the order of the two loops decides whether you are counting combinations or permutations.

39
Problems mapped
1
Easy
26
Medium
12
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The 1-D recurrence. for i: for c in range(w[i], C+1): dp[c] += dp[c - w[i]]. Capacity ascending. That is the only change from chapter 64, and it is what allows reuse.
  2. The loop-order rule — memorise this. Coins outer, capacity inner counts combinations (order does not matter): Coin Change II (518). Capacity outer, coins inner counts permutations (order matters): Combination Sum IV (377). Same recurrence, swapped loops, different answers. This is the single most-asked subtlety in the whole DP part.
  3. Why it works. With coins outer, each coin is considered exactly once and only in combination with previously-processed coins, so [1,2] and [2,1] are the same path. With capacity outer, each capacity can be reached by appending any coin last, so the two orders are different paths.
  4. Coin Change (322) is the minimum number of coins version: dp[c] = min(dp[c - coin] + 1). Initialise with inf, dp[0] = 0. Note that for minimisation the loop order does not matter (both give the same answer), but for counting it does.
  5. Perfect Squares (279) is 322 with the coins being perfect squares. Generate them with [i*i for i in range(1, isqrt(n)+1)].
  6. Word Break (139) is unbounded knapsack over dictionary words where the ‘capacity’ is a string prefix. dp[i] = 'the first i characters can be segmented'. The inner loop over words is O(len(words) * L) and is usually fast enough; a Trie or a max-word-length bound optimises it.
  7. Word Break II (140) adds reconstruction, which turns it into backtracking with memoisation on the suffix. Recognise when ‘count’ becomes ‘enumerate’.
  8. Integer Break (343), Minimum Cost For Tickets (983) and Count Ways To Build Good Strings (2466) are all unbounded selections over a set of ‘coins’ that are not literally coins.
  9. Maximum Number of Points with Cost (1937) and Frog Jump (403) are DP over a reachable set rather than a capacity; the state space is sparse, so a dict or a set beats an array.
  10. The recognition signal. ‘Unlimited supply’, ‘reuse’, ‘any number of times’, or a set of items you may draw from repeatedly. And whenever you see ‘number of ways’, stop and ask: does order matter? That question decides your loop order.
