DP – Subset Sum and Partitioning

The Kernel

A special case of knapsack where value equals weight, so the state is just a set of reachable sums. A bitset makes it one line in Python.

25
Problems mapped
1
Easy
15
Medium
9
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The reachable-sums DP. dp = [False] * (target + 1); dp[0] = True, then for x in nums: for s in range(target, x-1, -1): dp[s] |= dp[s-x]. Descending, because each number is used once.
  2. The bitset version. bits = 1; for x in nums: bits |= bits << x. Then bits >> target & 1 is the answer for 416. This is O(n * target / 64) and is dramatically faster in Python — it is the version to write if you want to impress.
  3. Partition Equal Subset Sum (416) is the canonical statement: total must be even and total // 2 must be reachable.
  4. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) is NP-hard in general, so it is backtracking (chapter 48), not DP. The DP works only when k = 2. Knowing why is a good interview moment.
  5. Matchsticks to Square (473) is 698 with k = 4. Same backtracking, same heuristics.
  6. Minimum Number of Work Sessions (1986) is subset-sum over bitmasks: dp[mask] = (sessions, time_in_last_session) as a tuple, minimised lexicographically. It is the bridge to chapter 73.
  7. Tallest Billboard (956) has a state of ‘the difference between the two sums’, which is a clever re-parameterisation: dp[d] = max total height with difference d. When the natural state is too large, re-parameterise by a difference or a ratio.
  8. Number of Ways to Split Array (2270) and Find the Array Concatenation Value-style problems are prefix-sum problems, not subset-sum — do not over-fit the pattern.
  9. Largest Multiple of Three (1363) is a greedy modulo problem, not a subset DP. The recognition: the target is a property of the whole selection (divisibility), and greedy by remainder class works.
  10. The recognition signal. ‘Can you partition’, ‘split into two equal’, ‘reach exactly’, ‘subset with sum’. If the numbers are large and n is small, it is backtracking; if the target is small and n is large, it is bitset DP. State which regime you are in — it is the deciding question.

Chapter 67

DP – Grid and Path DP

The Kernel

dp[r][c] = the best/count for reaching cell (r, c). It depends on the top and left neighbours. The extra top row and left column of zeros are the boundary conditions.

30
Problems mapped
0
Easy
19
Medium
11
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Unique Paths (62): dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1], with the first row and first column all 1. It is binomial coefficients in disguise — C(m+n-2, m-1) — which is the O(min(m,n)) follow-up.
  2. Unique Paths II (63) adds obstacles: set dp[r][c] = 0 where grid[r][c] == 1. The first-row/first-column initialisation must stop at the first obstacle, not skip it.
  3. Minimum Path Sum (64) changes + to min and adds grid[r][c]. Triangle (120) is the same DP on a ragged array, and iterating bottom-up avoids all boundary handling — that is the trick worth memorising.
  4. Minimum Falling Path Sum (931) has three predecessors (up-left, up, up-right). Minimum Falling Path Sum II (1289) removes the diagonal restriction, which naively becomes O(n^3); the optimisation is to track the two smallest values in the previous row, making it O(n^2). Tracking the best and second-best to avoid a forbidden choice is a reusable trick.
  5. Maximal Square (221): dp[r][c] = 1 + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]) when the cell is '1'. The min of three is the insight — it says ‘the largest square ending here is limited by the smallest of the three neighbours’. Count Square Submatrices (1277) is the same table summed instead of maximised.
  6. Cherry Pickup (741) is two walkers moving simultaneously: dp[steps][r1][r2] where c1 = steps - r1, c2 = steps - r2. The key reduction is that both walkers take the same number of steps, so one index is redundant. Cherry Pickup II (1463) is the same with two robots in different rows.
  7. Dungeon Game (174) is a backwards DP: compute the minimum health needed from each cell to the end, iterating from bottom-right to top-left. When the constraint must hold at every prefix, DP backwards.
  8. Out of Boundary Paths (576) and Knight Probability (688) are DP over a state (steps, r, c) — the step count is an explicit dimension because the answer depends on it.
  9. Rolling rows. Any grid DP that only looks one row up can be reduced to two rows. Maximal Square needs dp[r-1][c-1], so keep a prev_diag variable alongside a single row.
  10. Grid DP vs grid DFS. If the question asks for a count or an optimum over all paths, and moves are only in fixed directions, it is DP. If moves can go in all four directions, or you must not revisit cells, it is DFS/backtracking (chapter 49). The direction restriction is what makes DP possible — say this out loud, because it is exactly the question an interviewer asks.

Chapter 68

DP – Interval DP

The Kernel

dp[i][j] = the answer for the subarray i..j. You iterate by length, and the transition splits at a k in between. The classic trick is to think about what happens last, not first.

21
Problems mapped
0
Easy
10
Medium
11
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The loop skeleton. for length in range(2, n+1): for i in range(n-length+1): j = i + length - 1; for k in range(i, j): .... The outer loop is length, not i. Iterating by i computes cells before their dependencies exist. This is the single most important structural fact about interval DP.
  2. Think about the last operation, not the first. Burst Balloons (312) is impossible if you reason about which balloon to burst first (the subproblems are not independent). If you reason about which balloon is burst last, the left and right subarrays become independent and the DP works. This reframing is the entire problem, and it is the most valuable single idea in the DP part.
  3. The sentinel padding. For 312, pad the array with 1 at both ends so the boundary products are handled without special cases. For Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick (1547), pad the cut positions with 0 and n.
  4. Minimum Score Triangulation (1039) is 312 with a different cost function. Minimum Cost Tree From Leaf Values (1130) is the same shape with max instead of a sum, and has a monotonic stack solution as well — knowing both is a strong answer.
  5. Remove Boxes (546) needs a three-dimensional state dp[i][j][k] where k is the number of boxes of the same colour as a[i] attached to the left. Without k, the subproblems are not independent. It is the hardest interval DP in the book.
  6. Strange Printer (664) has the trick: if s[i] == s[k], you can print them in the same stroke, so dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k-1] + dp[k+1][j]). Recognising that equal endpoints can be merged into one operation is the reduction.
  7. Guess Number Higher or Lower II (375) is minimax interval DP: dp[i][j] = min over k of (k + max(dp[i][k-1], dp[k+1][j])). The min(max(...)) structure is what makes it a game problem.
  8. Palindrome Partitioning II (132) combines interval DP with a palindrome precomputation. dp[i] = minimum cuts for the prefix; the inner loop checks palindromic suffixes. Precomputing is_pal[i][j] in O(n^2) is what makes it O(n^2) instead of O(n^3).
  9. Scramble String (87) is interval DP on a 3-D state (two intervals plus a length) with memoisation. It is a good example of the state being richer than (i, j).
  10. Complexity is O(n^3) for the basic shape. With n <= 100 that is 10^6 operations and fine; with n <= 500 you need a better idea. Read the constraints to decide whether interval DP is even admissible.
  11. The recognition signal. The input is a sequence, the operation consumes or merges elements, and the order of operations matters. ‘Burst’, ‘merge’, ‘cut’, ‘remove’, ‘partition with a cost’ — all interval DP.

Chapter 69

DP – State Machine (The Stock Family)

The Kernel

At each day the trader is in one of a small number of states (holding or not, and how many transactions used). Write one recurrence per state. The whole stock family is one template with a different number of states.

21
Problems mapped
1
Easy
12
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Two states, unlimited transactions (122): hold = max(hold, cash - price), cash = max(cash, hold + price). Iterate the two updates carefully — using the new hold in the cash update lets you buy and sell on the same day. Use the old values: hold, cash = max(hold, cash - p), max(cash, hold + p) as a tuple assignment evaluates the right-hand side first, which is exactly what you want.
  2. One transaction only (121): buy = min(buy, price), profit = max(profit, price - buy). Two variables, no dp array.
  3. At most two transactions (123): four variables — buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2 — with the chain buy1 = max(buy1, -p), sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p), buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - p), sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p). Again, the tuple assignment order matters and is why the chain works in one pass.
  4. At most k transactions (188): the same chain generalised to arrays buy[j] and sell[j] for j in 1..k. If k >= n // 2 the answer is the unlimited case — that early return is what keeps the complexity at O(n * min(k, n/2)).
  5. With a cooldown (309): three states — hold, sold, rest. The transition is hold = max(hold, rest - p), rest = max(rest, sold), sold = hold_old + p. The extra rest state is what encodes the one-day gap.
  6. With a transaction fee (714): subtract the fee on either the buy or the sell, but not both. Subtracting on the sell is the usual choice: cash = max(cash, hold + price - fee).
  7. The four-line template for the whole family. for p in prices: buy = max(buy, prev_state - p); sell = max(sell, buy + p); prev_state = .... Every variant in this chapter is a different definition of prev_state.
  8. Generalising beyond stocks. Any problem where you are ‘in a mode’ that changes what moves are legal is a state machine: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee, Student Attendance Record II (552), Number of Ways to Paint N x 3 Grid (1411), Count Vowels Permutation (1220). Recognise the shared shape.
  9. State machines beat ‘prefix/suffix max’ solutions. Many stock problems also have a clever prefix-suffix-array solution for the two-transaction case, but it does not generalise to k. The state machine generalises, so lead with it.
  10. The recognition signal. ‘Buy’, ‘sell’, ‘hold’, ‘cooldown’, ‘fee’, ‘at most k transactions’, or any problem with an explicit mode that restricts the next action.

DP – Tree DP

The Kernel

Postorder returns a small tuple of values summarising the subtree; the parent combines its children’s tuples. The state lives in the return value, not in a table.

21
Problems mapped
1
Easy
12
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The return value is the state. For House Robber III (337) the return is (rob_this, skip_this) — a two-tuple. The parent computes rob = node.val + left.skip + right.skip and skip = max(left.rob, left.skip) + max(right.rob, right.skip). Writing two separate recursive functions instead of one returning a tuple is the usual first attempt and is O(n^2).
  2. Returning a tuple is the general technique. Whenever a node needs more than one piece of information from its subtree, return a tuple. Common tuples: (rob, skip), (height, diameter), (min, max, size), (is_bst, min, max, sum).
  3. Binary Tree Cameras (968) returns a three-state enum: covered-with-camera, covered-without-camera, uncovered. The greedy assignment rule (place a camera at the parent of any uncovered node) falls out of the postorder. It is the hardest tree DP in the book.
  4. Largest BST Subtree (333) returns (is_bst, min_val, max_val, size). The min/max are needed so the parent can check the BST property — returning only the size is not enough. This is the standard example of why the return value must be sufficient.
  5. Diameter (543) and Max Path Sum (124) return one value and update a nonlocal best — the hybrid from chapter 41. They are tree DP in the loose sense: the state is one number.
  6. Distribute Coins (979) returns the net excess and accumulates abs() into a global. The return value is a deficit, which is the insight.
  7. Most Frequent Subtree Sum (508) returns the sum and accumulates a Counter. Longest ZigZag Path (1372) returns a two-tuple (left-going, right-going). Maximum Average Subtree (1120) returns (sum, count).
  8. Sum of Distances in Tree (834) is the flagship hard tree DP: compute subtree sizes and the answer for the root in one postorder, then reroot in a second pass. The rerooting formula ans[child] = ans[parent] + n - 2 * size[child] is worth memorising — it is the standard ‘all nodes as root’ technique.
  9. Count Nodes With the Same Label (1519) combines tree DP with a per-label running count. Number of Good Leaf Nodes Pairs (1530) returns a list of depths.
  10. Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum and Diameter are the two tree DP problems you are most likely to be asked. If you only memorise two, memorise those, plus House Robber III as the tuple-returning archetype.

DP – Palindrome DP

The Kernel

dp[i][j] = whether/how s[i..j] is a palindrome, computed by increasing length. Once you have the table, every palindrome problem is a second DP or a greedy on top of it.

27
Problems mapped
8
Easy
9
Medium
10
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The palindrome table. is_pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or is_pal[i+1][j-1]). Iterate i descending and j ascending (or iterate by length) so that is_pal[i+1][j-1] is already computed.
  2. Longest Palindromic Substring (5) tracks the maximum j - i + 1 over the table. The expand-around-centre solution is O(n^2) time and O(1) space and is shorter — know both, and note that Manacher’s algorithm gets O(n).
  3. Palindromic Substrings (647) counts the True cells. Expand-around-centre is again the shorter solution.
  4. Longest Palindromic Subsequence (516) is not the same as the substring: it is LCS of the string with its reverse, or equivalently dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 if the ends match, else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Note the difference from the substring version: subsequence takes a max, substring resets to False.
  5. Palindrome Partitioning II (132) needs the palindrome table plus a 1-D dp[i] = minimum cuts for the prefix. The two-layer structure (table then DP) is the standard composition for palindrome problems.
  6. Palindrome Partitioning III (1278) is 132 with a fixed number of cuts — a two-dimensional DP over (prefix, cuts_used) on top of the palindrome table. Three layers, but each is simple.
  7. Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome (1312) is n - LPS(s). That identity is worth memorising: insertions needed = length minus longest palindromic subsequence.
  8. Valid Palindrome III (1216) is 'can it become a palindrome with at most k deletions', which is n - LPS <= k. Same identity.
  9. Shortest Palindrome (214) needs KMP: the answer is the string prepended with the reverse of the part that is not a palindromic prefix. The KMP failure function on s + '#' + s[::-1] gives the longest palindromic prefix. It is a chapter 83 problem that lives here by topic.
  10. Construct K Palindrome Strings (1400) is a counting argument, not a DP: at most n palindromes, at least the number of characters with an odd count.
  11. The expand-around-centre function, memorised. for c in range(2*n - 1): l, r = c // 2, c // 2 + c % 2; while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]: l -= 1; r += 1. Handling both odd and even centres in one loop is the trick.
  12. Recognition signal. The word ‘palindrome’ plus ‘longest’, ‘count’, ‘partition’, or ‘minimum cuts’. All of them start with the same table.

DP – Game Theory and Minimax

The Kernel

dp[i][j] is the advantage (current player’s score minus the opponent’s) obtainable from the interval. The recurrence is max(take_left - dp[i+1][j], take_right - dp[i][j-1]) — note the minus, which flips the perspective.

23
Problems mapped
4
Easy
10
Medium
9
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The advantage formulation is the key trick. Define dp[i][j] as current_player_score - other_player_score for the subarray i..j. Then dp[i][j] = max(a[i] - dp[i+1][j], a[j] - dp[i][j-1]). The subtraction encodes ‘after I take, my opponent faces the same problem and their advantage is my disadvantage’. Deriving this recurrence is the entire insight — the naive ‘maximise my total’ formulation requires tracking both scores and is much harder.
  2. The win condition. Predict the Winner (486) is dp[0][n-1] >= 0. Stone Game (877) is always True for even-length arrays — that observation (the first player can always take all odd-indexed or all even-indexed piles) is the intended ‘solution’ and is worth stating.
  3. Space optimisation. The advantage DP only needs two rows, so it can be done with a 1-D array of length n iterated correctly. Offer it as the follow-up.
  4. Stone Game II (1140) has state (index, M) — the number of piles you may take depends on M, which changes. Stone Game III (1406) is a 1-D advantage DP. Stone Game VII (1690) uses the sum of the remaining interval as the gain and the advantage DP as the structure.
  5. Can I Win (464) is minimax over a bitmask of used numbers — it is chapter 73’s bitmask DP with a game recurrence. State (mask) -> can current player win.
  6. Guess Number Higher or Lower II (375) is minimax where the current player chooses the pivot and the adversary chooses the outcome: dp[i][j] = min over k of (k + max(dp[i][k-1], dp[k+1][j])). The min(max(...)) is the signature of a minimax with adversarial choice.
  7. Cat and Mouse (913) and Cat and Mouse II (1728) are game DP over a joint state with three outcomes (win, lose, draw). The draw condition makes them harder than the standard minimax and requires cycle-aware evaluation.
  8. Nim-style problems (292, 1025, 1908) are not DP: the answer is a parity or a modulo condition. Nim Game (292) is n % 4 != 0; Divisor Game (1025) is n % 2 == 0. Always check for the closed form before writing a DP — interviewers ask these to see whether you over-engineer.
  9. Predict the Winner with a greedy is wrong. There is a tempting ‘always take the larger end’ greedy and it fails. If you propose it, produce the counterexample.
  10. Recognition signal. Two players, alternating turns, perfect play, optimal strategy, and a question about who wins or by how much. The advantage formulation applies whenever the game is zero-sum and the state is an interval or a mask.

DP – Bitmask DP

The Kernel

When n <= 20, the state is a subset, and a subset is an integer. dp[mask] = the answer for the subset mask. Iterate masks in increasing order so every subset is computed before its supersets.

26
Problems mapped
0
Easy
8
Medium
18
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The n <= 20 signal. 2^20 is about a million states, which is the upper limit of comfortable bitmask DP. If n <= 20, think bitmask; if n <= 12, an O(2^n * n^2) transition is fine; if n <= 25, you need meet-in-the-middle instead.
  2. Enumerating the set bits of a mask. while m: b = m & -m; i = b.bit_length() - 1; m ^= b. Or simply for i in range(n): if mask >> i & 1. The m & -m idiom extracts the lowest set bit and is worth knowing.
  3. Enumerating submasks. sub = mask; while sub: ...; sub = (sub - 1) & mask. This enumerates all submasks in O(3^n) total, which is the standard technique for subset-partition DP (1723, 1601, 2741).
  4. Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes (847): BFS over (node, visited_mask); the answer is the first state where mask == (1 << n) - 1. It is BFS, not DP, but the state is a bitmask — recognise the shared representation.
  5. Smallest Sufficient Team (1125): dp[mask] = the smallest team covering the skill set mask. The transition tries each person and ORs their skill mask. The ‘people as items, skills as the subset’ framing is the reduction.
  6. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) and Minimum Number of Work Sessions (1986) use dp[mask] = (sessions, time_in_last) as a tuple minimised lexicographically. Tuple-valued DP states are common in this chapter.
  7. Maximum AND Sum of Array (2172) assigns numbers to slots with capacity 2 — the state is which slots are filled. Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats (1434) is subset DP over hats with a people-mask.
  8. Stickers to Spell Word (691) memoises on the remaining target string, which is a compressed state. When the subset is a set of letters rather than indices, a Counter or a string is the state.
  9. Find the Shortest Superstring (943) is TSP on strings: dp[mask][i] = shortest superstring ending at i, with an overlap precomputation. It is the canonical ‘bitmask DP for ordering’ problem.
  10. Minimum Incompatibility (1681) and Maximize Score After N Operations (1799) are subset-partition DP with a validity check per subset. Precompute the valid subsets first, then DP.
  11. Count Number of Maximum Bitwise-OR Subsets (2044) and Sum of All Subset XOR Totals (1863) have closed forms or simple enumerations — check before reaching for DP.
  12. The generic shape. dp[mask] = best over i not in mask of f(dp[mask | (1 << i)], cost(mask, i)). If your transition looks like that, you have bitmask DP; the only work left is defining cost.

Part XII · Dynamic Programming
Chapter 74

DP – Digit DP

The Kernel

Count numbers in [0, N] satisfying a digit property by processing the digits left to right with a tight flag. The state is (position, tight, ...).

18
Problems mapped
0
Easy
6
Medium
12
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The tight flag. tight means 'the prefix so far equals the prefix of N', so the current digit is capped at N[pos]. When tight is true the digit may equal N[pos]; otherwise it may be 0-9 freely. This one boolean is the entire idea of digit DP.
  2. The recursive shape. f(pos, tight, state) where state carries whatever property you are tracking (last digit, whether a repeat occurred, the digit count). Memoise on (pos, tight, state). The tight=True states are never revisited, so you may exclude them from the cache — a common optimisation.
  3. The started flag. If leading zeros are not real digits, you need a second boolean for ‘has the number started’. Number of Digit One (233) and Count Special Integers (2376) both need it. Forgetting it produces counts that treat 007 as a three-digit number.
  4. Number of Digit One (233) is the flagship: count the occurrences of the digit 1 across all numbers in [0, n]. There is also a beautiful O(log n) closed form counting per digit position, and knowing both is the ideal answer.
  5. Numbers With Repeated Digits (1012) is ‘count numbers with no repeated digit’ via the complementary count. Count Special Integers (2376) is the same problem restated. Numbers At Most N Given Digit Set (902) restricts the allowed digits, which removes the tight-only branching.
  6. Non-negative Integers without Consecutive Ones (600) tracks the last digit in the state. Count Numbers with Unique Digits (357) has a closed form (9 9 8 * ... ) and is a good warm-up.
  7. Number of Beautiful Integers in the Range (2827) and Count the Number of Powerful Integers (2999) are modern digit DP problems with richer states (digit-sum parity, suffix constraints).
  8. Range queries are f(R) - f(L-1). Every 'in the range [L, R]' digit problem is two prefix counts. That reduction is always the first line.
  9. The iterative alternative. 233 and 902 can be done by iterating digit positions and counting completions combinatorially, which is O(log n) and often shorter than the recursive DP. If you can derive the combinatorial count, prefer it — interviewers reward the closed form.
  10. Recognition signal. 'Count numbers in [0, N] such that the digits satisfy ...', with N up to 10^9 or 10^18. The constraint size (N huge, n irrelevant) is the giveaway: the complexity must be in the number of digits, not the value.

Greedy

Part XIII · Greedy
Chapter 75

Greedy – Sort First

The Kernel

If the optimal solution can be built by repeatedly taking the best remaining item under some order, sort by the right key and sweep once. The whole problem is choosing the sort key.

66
Problems mapped
15
Easy
43
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Choosing the sort key is the entire problem. Sort by the constraint (deadline, end time, capacity), not by the value, when the constraint is what runs out.
  2. Intervals: sort by end to remove, sort by start to merge. Non-overlapping Intervals (435) and Minimum Number of Arrows (452) sort by end and greedily keep the earliest-finishing interval. Merge Intervals (56) sorts by start. Getting these backwards produces a plausible but wrong answer, so state your key and your justification explicitly.
  3. Assign Cookies (455): sort both; two pointers; give the smallest cookie that satisfies the least greedy child. The greedy is ‘do not waste a large cookie on a small child’.
  4. Array Partition (561) is ‘sort and sum every second element’. The proof is an exchange argument and is worth being able to sketch.
  5. Two City Scheduling (1029) sorts by the difference costA - costB and sends the first n to A. Sorting by a difference is the standard technique when each item has two competing costs.
  6. Maximum Units on a Truck (1710) and Boats to Save People (881) sort by value density and by weight respectively, then sweep with a two-pointer.
  7. Task Scheduler (621) has a closed-form greedy: (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) + count_of_max_freq and then max(result, len(tasks)). The max with len(tasks) is required for the case where there are enough distinct tasks to fill every gap.
  8. Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended (1353) is the flagship sort-plus-heap greedy: sort by start day, and use a min-heap of end days to always attend the event that expires soonest.
  9. Minimum Number of Refueling Stops (871) is a greedy with a max-heap: drive as far as possible, and when stuck, retroactively add the largest fuel station passed. The ‘retroactive choice’ pattern — making a decision about the past when you learn new information — is a recurring greedy technique.
  10. Course Schedule III (630) is the same retroactive pattern: add every course, and when the total duration exceeds a deadline, drop the longest course (max-heap).
  11. Furthest Building You Can Reach (1642) is the same: use ladders on the largest gaps, bricks on the rest.
  12. Partition Labels (763) is a two-pass greedy: record each character’s last index, then extend the current partition’s end to the maximum last index seen. No sorting needed.
  13. The proof obligation. A greedy answer needs an exchange argument: 'suppose an optimal solution differs from the greedy choice at the first point; swapping the greedy choice in does not make it worse.' Being able to state that sentence is often worth more than the code.

Chapter 76

Greedy – Reachability and Exchange Arguments

The Kernel

Track a single scalar — the furthest reach, the current fuel, the current coverage — and update it with a bound. These problems look like DP and are not.

87
Problems mapped
14
Easy
57
Medium
16
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Jump Game (55): keep reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]); if i > reach at any point, return False. Check the failure condition before the update** — the loop must verify that the current index is reachable before extending.
  2. Jump Game II (45): BFS in disguise. Track cur_end and farthest; when i == cur_end, increment the jump count and set cur_end = farthest. The ‘level end’ variable is what makes it a BFS** — recognising that is the insight.
  3. Jump Game III (1306) and Jump Game IV (1345) are BFS/DFS, not greedy — the jumps can go backwards, which destroys the reachability monotonicity. Recognise when a ‘jump’ problem is actually a graph problem.
  4. Gas Station (134): if the total gas is at least the total cost, a solution exists; the start is the index after the last point where the running tank went negative. Both facts must be stated** — the existence condition and the start-index rule.
  5. Minimum Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden (1326) is Jump Game II after converting intervals into reach values. The reduction from intervals to a reach array is the whole problem.
  6. Video Stitching (1024) is 1326 with a different framing — again, convert intervals to a farthest[i] array and run the jump algorithm.
  7. Patching Array (330): maintain miss = the smallest sum you cannot form. If nums[i] <= miss, extend miss += nums[i]; otherwise patch with miss and double it. The invariant miss is the smallest unreachable sum** — state it, and the algorithm is obvious.
  8. Candy (135) is a two-pass greedy: left-to-right enforcing the increasing rule, then right-to-left enforcing the decreasing rule, taking the maximum. Two passes because each direction is independent.
  9. Trapping Rain Water (42) has the two-pointer greedy from chapter 5 — track left_max and right_max and always advance the shorter side. It is a greedy, not a DP, and that is worth saying.
  10. Container With Most Water (11) is the same greedy: always move the shorter wall. The proof is that moving the taller wall can never increase the area, because the shorter wall is the binding constraint.
  11. Maximum Subarray with a greedy is Kadane (chapter 61) — a greedy and a DP that coincide. When a greedy and a DP agree, prefer the greedy for code length and mention the DP for correctness.

Chapter 77

Greedy – Heap-Assisted Choice

The Kernel

When the greedy needs ‘the best available among the currently eligible’, maintain a heap of eligible candidates. This is the bridge between greedy and scheduling.

33
Problems mapped
0
Easy
22
Medium
11
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The universal shape. Sort by one key to control eligibility, push eligible items into a heap keyed by the greedy criterion, then pop when you must commit. The sort controls when, the heap controls which.
  2. Task Scheduler (621) has both a closed form and a heap simulation. Write the closed form; mention the simulation.
  3. IPO (502) is the canonical two-phase version: sort projects by capital, push every now-affordable project into a max-heap by profit, pop the best, repeat. The while loop that pushes all newly affordable projects before each pop is the key structure.
  4. Reorganize String (767) and Longest Happy String (1405) use a max-heap by remaining count plus a ‘hold the previous item aside for one step’ buffer. The buffer is what prevents an immediate repeat.
  5. Course Schedule III (630) and Minimum Number of Refueling Stops (871) are retroactive greedy: take everything, then undo the worst choice when the constraint is violated. The heap holds the undo candidates.
  6. Furthest Building You Can Reach (1642) is the same retroactive shape with a min-heap of gaps and a ladder budget.
  7. Maximum Performance of a Team (1383) sorts by efficiency and maintains a min-heap of speeds of size k, tracking efficiency sum_of_top_k_speeds. The state you track is a product*, which is what makes the problem non-obvious.
  8. Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended II (1751) is not a heap greedy — it is DP after sorting by end time with binary search for the previous compatible event. Recognising when the greedy breaks (overlapping events with weights) is important: weighted interval scheduling is DP, not greedy.
  9. Meeting Rooms II (253) is the simplest version: a min-heap of end times, push the new start, and if the earliest end is <= start, reuse the room.
  10. Divide Intervals Into Minimum Number of Groups (2406) is 253 with a different phrasing. Single-Threaded CPU (1834) and Number of the Smallest Unoccupied Chair (1942) are the same eligibility-plus-heap shape with extra state.
  11. Recognition signal. ‘Maximum profit given a budget’, ‘minimum number of X to cover Y’, ‘schedule to maximise Z’, with a resource that is consumed. If the choice set grows over time, sort plus heap.

Part XIV · Bits, Maths & Strings
Chapter 78

Bit Manipulation

The Kernel

Seven operations cover every bit problem: x & -x (lowest set bit), x & (x-1) (clear it), x ^ x = 0, x >> i & 1 (test), x | (1 << i) (set), x & ~(1 << i) (clear), x ^ (1 << i) (flip).

52
Problems mapped
26
Easy
22
Medium
4
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. So n & (n-1) == 0 is the power-of-two test (231), and looping it counts set bits (191). Power of Two (231) must also check n > 0 — zero passes the bit test and is not a power of two.
  2. x & -x isolates the lowest set bit. Use it to iterate set bits, and use it in Single Number III (260): XOR everything to get a ^ b, isolate any differing bit, then partition the array by that bit and XOR each half separately.
  3. XOR properties. a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a, XOR is commutative and associative. Therefore XORing an array where every element appears twice except one leaves the single element (136). This is the most-asked bit trick in interviews.
  4. Single Number II (137) breaks the XOR trick because elements appear three times. The answer is a bitwise count mod 3: sum the bits at each position across all numbers and take mod 3. The ones/twos state machine is the O(1)-space version.
  5. Missing Number (268) is XOR of range(n+1) with the array, or the Gauss sum. Find the Difference (389) and Set Mismatch (645) are the same XOR-all trick.
  6. Counting Bits (338) is dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1), or dp[i] = dp[i & (i-1)] + 1. Both are one-liners in a loop.
  7. Bitwise AND of Numbers Range (201)**: find the common prefix of left and right by right-shifting both until they are equal, then shift back. The answer is that prefix. Recognising that the AND of a range is the common binary prefix is the insight.
  8. Sum of Two Integers (371) without +: while b: carry = (a & b) << 1; a ^= b; b = carry. In Python this loops forever on negative numbers because of arbitrary precision — you must mask to 32 bits and convert back at the end. Python-specific gotcha, and a favourite interview question.
  9. Reverse Bits (190) and Number of 1 Bits (191) are the mechanical warm-ups.
  10. Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (421) uses a prefix-trie of bits built greedily from the top bit down. It is a Trie problem (chapter 83’s cousin) in bit clothing.
  11. Divide Two Integers (29) is bit-shift long division with a 32-bit clamp. The clamp to [-2^31, 2^31 - 1] is required and is the part candidates forget.
  12. Minimum Bit Flips (2220) is bin(a ^ b).count('1'). Total Hamming Distance (477) counts, per bit position, ones * zeros and sums. The ‘count per bit position’ reframing is the key technique — it converts a quadratic problem into a linear one.
  13. Python specifics. bin(x).count('1') is popcount; x.bit_length() gives the position of the highest set bit; int.bit_count() exists in Python 3.10+ and is the idiomatic answer.

Chapter 79

Bitmask Enumeration

The Kernel

Enumerate all 2^n subsets with for mask in range(1 << n) and test membership with mask >> i & 1. This is brute force made tidy, and it is often the intended solution when n <= 20.

23
Problems mapped
1
Easy
10
Medium
12
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The loop. for mask in range(1 << n): for i in range(n): if mask >> i & 1: .... In Python, [i for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1] is a clean inner expression.
  2. Gray code (89) generates an ordering where consecutive masks differ by one bit: i ^ (i >> 1). That single expression is the whole problem, and it is worth memorising.
  3. Sum of All Subset XOR Totals (1863) has a closed form: each bit contributes to 2^(n-1) subsets, so the answer is OR_of_all * 2^(n-1). Always look for the closed form before enumerating.
  4. Count Number of Maximum Bitwise-OR Subsets (2044) requires the OR of the full array first, then a count of subsets achieving it. The enumeration is O(2^n) and is intended.
  5. Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique Characters (1239) is subset enumeration with a validity pre-check per string and a bitmask of used letters. Encoding ‘letters used’ as a 26-bit mask turns the duplicate check into mask & other == 0 — that is the trick.
  6. Maximum Product of Word Lengths (318) is the same 26-bit letter mask idea: two words share no letter iff mask_a & mask_b == 0.
  7. Letter Case Permutation (784) is 2^(number of letters) enumerations where bit i selects the case of the i-th letter. It is cleaner than backtracking here.
  8. Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats (1434), Smallest Sufficient Team (1125) and Maximum AND Sum of Array (2172) are bitmask DP (chapter 73), not enumeration — the distinction is whether you memoise on the mask.
  9. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (698) is enumeration with pruning; 1601 (Maximum Number of Achievable Transfer Requests) is enumeration over request subsets with a net-degree check. Both are O(2^n) with n <= 16.
  10. Meet in the middle. When n is around 30-40, 2^n is too large but 2^(n/2) is fine: enumerate both halves and combine with a hash or a sort. Closest Subsequence Sum (1755) and Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference (2035) are the canonical meet-in-the-middle problems.
  11. Recognition signal. n <= 20 in the constraints, plus ‘subset’, ‘choose a group’, or ‘all combinations’. If you see n <= 20, bitmask is usually intended.

Chapter 80

Number Theory Essentials

The Kernel

Four tools: the sieve of Eratosthenes, gcd/lcm, modular exponentiation, and factorisation by trial division up to sqrt(n).

98
Problems mapped
46
Easy
48
Medium
4
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Sieve of Eratosthenes. is_prime = [True] (n+1); for i in 2..isqrt(n), if prime, mark multiples from ii off. Start at ii, not 2i — smaller multiples were already marked, and starting at i*i is the standard optimisation. Count Primes (204) is the archetype.
  2. Trial division. for d in range(2, isqrt(n) + 1) — the isqrt bound is mandatory or you are O(n). Use math.isqrt for exact integer square roots; int(n ** 0.5) has floating-point errors at large n.
  3. GCD and LCM. math.gcd(a, b) and a // gcd(a, b) b. Compute LCM as a // gcd b, not a * b // gcd — the latter overflows in fixed-width languages and is the standard style point.
  4. Euclid’s algorithm should be reproducible by hand: while b: a, b = b, a % b; return a. GCD of Strings (1071) is s + t == t + s plus the string of length gcd(len(s), len(t)) — a beautiful non-numeric use of the same idea.
  5. Fast modular exponentiation. pow(base, exp, mod) is built into Python and is the answer for Pow(x, n) (50) in its integer form. For the floating-point version, square-and-multiply by hand: while n: if n & 1: result = base; base = base; n >>= 1.
  6. Ugly Number II (264) is not a number-theory problem — it is three-pointer merging of three generated sequences. Super Ugly Number (313) generalises to k pointers, and a heap also works. Recognise the merge.
  7. Ugly Number III (1201) is the counting version and uses inclusion-exclusion plus binary search (chapter 14). Three tools stacked.
  8. Modular arithmetic. (a + b) % m, (a * b) % m, and for division you need the modular inverse via Fermat’s little theorem (pow(a, m-2, m) when m is prime). Problems that say ‘modulo 10^9+7’ and require division need this.
  9. Factorial Trailing Zeroes (172) is a counting problem: the number of factors of 5, computed as n//5 + n//25 + n//125 + .... No factorial is ever computed.
  10. Max Points on a Line (149) is a geometry problem using gcd to normalise slope fractions so they can be hashed. Normalising a ratio by its gcd before hashing is the reusable technique.
  11. Water and Jug Problem (365) is a number-theory problem in disguise: the answer is target % gcd(x, y) == 0 and target <= x + y. Recognising Bézout’s identity is the whole solution.
  12. Perfect Number (507), Self Dividing Numbers (728) and Count Odd Numbers in an Interval Range (1523) are arithmetic warm-ups — do not over-engineer them.
  13. Bit counting and bases. bin, oct, hex for output; int(s, base) for input; divmod for digit extraction. Excel Sheet Column Number (171) is base-26 with a twist.

Math Simulation and Big Numbers

The Kernel

When the numbers exceed the language’s integer range, or the problem is a step-by-step simulation, do the arithmetic digit by digit in an array with an explicit carry.

92
Problems mapped
34
Easy
48
Medium
10
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Multiply Strings (43) and Add Strings (415) and Add Binary (67) are one template: two pointers from the least significant digit, an accumulator, divmod for digit and carry, then reverse. Python’s arbitrary-precision integers mean you can cheat with str(int(a) * int(b)) — offer the honest digit-by-digit version first, then mention that Python makes it a one-liner. Interviewers accept both, but the honest version is what is being tested.
  2. Plus One (66) is the carry template on a single array, with the all-nines edge case prepending a 1.
  3. Reverse Integer (7) and String to Integer (atoi) (8) are careful-parsing problems. 7 has an overflow clamp; 8 has a multi-clause specification (whitespace, sign, non-digits, clamp). For 8, enumerate the clauses out loud before coding — it is a specification-reading test, not an algorithm test.
  4. Integer to English Words (273) is a lookup-table recursion over thousands, millions, billions. The three ifs (hundreds, tens, teens) are where the bugs are.
  5. Integer to Roman (12) and Roman to Integer (13) are lookup tables. For 12, the greedy over a descending value list including the subtractive pairs (900, 400, 90, 40, 9, 4) is the clean solution.
  6. Zigzag Conversion (6) is a simulation with a direction flag and a 2 * numRows - 2 period. Recognising the period removes the need for nested lists of rows.
  7. Count and Say (38) is a pure simulation: run-length encode the previous term. Use itertools.groupby or a manual two-pointer count.
  8. Pascal’s Triangle (118, 119)**: row[i] += row[i-1] right-to-left in place. 119 asks for a single row, which the in-place right-to-left update gives you with O(k) space.
  9. Spiral Matrix, Rotate Image, Set Matrix Zeroes are simulations covered in chapter 58. Game of Life (289) is the in-place bit encoding from that chapter.
  10. Fizz Buzz (412), Add Digits (258), Nim Game (292), Bulb Switcher (319) are warm-ups with closed forms. 319 is ‘count the perfect squares up to n’ — the insight is that only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors.
  11. Minimum Moves to Equal Array Elements (453) is sum(a) - n * min(a). The reduction ‘increment n-1 elements’ equals ‘decrement 1 element’ is the whole problem.
  12. Distribute Candies to People (1103) and similar are pure simulations; do not look for a formula unless the constraints force it.
  13. Recognition signal. ‘Without using built-in big integers’, ‘the result may be very large’, or a problem with many explicit specification clauses. Read the specification twice and enumerate the cases before coding.

Chapter 82

String – Palindromes, Pointers, and Parsing

The Kernel

Most string problems are array problems where the elements happen to be characters. The only genuinely string-specific tools are the frequency count, the two-pointer palindrome check, and the character-class predicate.

135
Problems mapped
80
Easy
48
Medium
7
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Palindrome check. s == s[::-1] for a copy, or the two-pointer loop for O(1) space. Valid Palindrome (125) requires filtering to alphanumerics first — c.isalnum() and c.lower().
  2. Valid Palindrome II (680) allows one deletion: on the first mismatch, try skipping the left character or the right character and check whether either remainder is a palindrome. Only the first mismatch needs handling — a second mismatch means both branches fail.
  3. Longest Palindrome (409) is a counting argument: 2 * sum(count // 2 for count in Counter(s).values()) plus 1 if any count is odd. No construction needed.
  4. Reverse String (344) and Reverse Words in a String (151) are pointer exercises. For 151, ' '.join(s.split()[::-1]) is the one-liner — split() with no argument handles all whitespace runs.
  5. Is Subsequence (392) is a two-pointer scan, or bisect over per-character index lists for the follow-up ‘many queries’ version.
  6. String Compression (443) is the read/write pointer pattern from chapter 6, writing both the character and its count digits in place.
  7. Zigzag, atoi, Count and Say and the arithmetic string problems are in chapter 81 — string parsing with explicit specifications.
  8. Remove All Adjacent Duplicates (1047, 1209), Make The String Great (1544) and Backspace String Compare (844) are stack problems (chapter 29).
  9. Word Pattern (290) and Isomorphic Strings (205) are bijection checks (chapter 21).
  10. Decode String (394), Basic Calculator (224, 227) and Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (150) are stack-based parsers (chapter 25).
  11. Character-class predicates worth knowing. c.isalpha(), c.isdigit(), c.isalnum(), c.isspace(), c.isupper(). And for conversion: ord(c), chr(i), int(c), str(i).
  12. Never build a string with += in a loop — it is O(n^2) in Python because strings are immutable. Use a list and ''.join(parts). This is a real performance issue on LeetCode’s larger test cases and a standard style point.
  13. str.translate and str.maketrans do character-level replacement in one C-level call — useful for Ransom Note-style substitutions and worth knowing.

Part XIV · Bits, Maths & Strings
Chapter 83

String – KMP and the Z-Algorithm

The Kernel

KMP precomputes, for every prefix, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. That table makes pattern matching O(n + m) and answers a surprising number of ‘repeated structure’ questions.

17
Problems mapped
4
Easy
4
Medium
9
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The failure function. lps[i] = the length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also a suffix. Build it with two pointers: i scanning and j the current matched length, with the fallback j = lps[j-1] on mismatch. The fallback is the whole algorithm — without it you are back to brute force.
  2. Matching uses the same fallback: on a mismatch after j matches, set j = lps[j-1] and do not advance i. That 'do not advance i' is what makes it linear.
  3. Find the Index of the First Occurrence (28) is the direct application. In Python, s.find(t) is the one-liner and uses a C-optimised search — but the interviewer is asking for KMP, so write it.
  4. Repeated Substring Pattern (459) has a one-line answer: s in (s + s)[1:-1]. The reasoning is that a repeated string appears in its own doubled version. Knowing this trick is a strong signal; knowing the KMP version too is stronger.
  5. Shortest Palindrome (214) uses lps on s + '#' + s[::-1] to find the longest palindromic prefix, then prepends the reverse of the rest. The '#' separator prevents the prefix from crossing the boundary.
  6. Longest Happy Prefix (1392) is literally lps[-1] — the definition of the failure function’s last value.
  7. Find the Longest Substring Containing Vowels in Even Counts (1371) uses a bitmask prefix state, not KMP, but lives in the same mental neighbourhood.
  8. The Z-array. z[i] = the length of the longest common prefix of s and s[i:]. It answers the same questions as KMP with a different precomputation. The [l, r] window optimisation is what makes it linear.
  9. When to use which. KMP when you need the failure function for s + '#' + t; Z when you need all prefix matches at once. Both are O(n); pick whichever you can write faster.
  10. Rolling hash is the alternative (chapter 84). It is shorter to write but has collision risk; KMP is exact. If the interviewer asks for ‘linear time string matching’, either is acceptable, but say which and why.
  11. Recognition signal. ‘Find the pattern in the text’, ‘longest repeated substring’, ‘shortest palindrome by prepending’, ‘the string is a repetition of a substring’. All of them are the failure function.

Chapter 84

String – Rolling Hash and Substring Search

The Kernel

Hash every substring in O(1) from the previous one: h = (h * base + code(c)) % mod. With prefix hashes you can compare any two substrings in O(1).

22
Problems mapped
3
Easy
10
Medium
9
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Prefix-hash construction. pre[i+1] = (pre[i] base + code(s[i])) % mod, and pow_base[i] = base^i % mod. Then the hash of s[l:r] is (pre[r] - pre[l] pow_base[r-l]) % mod.
  2. Collisions. A single 64-bit modulus is usually enough for competitive programming, but for an interview you should mention the collision risk and offer double hashing (two different moduli) or a verification step. Saying ‘this is probabilistic’ is the point being tested.
  3. Repeated DNA Sequences (187) is the simplest case: a 10-character window over a 4-letter alphabet, which fits in 20 bits. Use a bit-shift rolling hash and a set of seen hashes.
  4. Longest Duplicate Substring (1044) is binary search on the length plus a rolling-hash set. The binary search is monotone because if a duplicate substring of length L exists, one of length L-1 does too. This is the flagship rolling-hash problem and it combines chapters 13, 84 and 22.
  5. Maximum Length of Repeated Subarray (718) can be solved with DP (chapter 63) or rolling hash plus binary search. The DP is simpler; the hash is faster for large inputs.
  6. Distinct Echo Substrings (1147) and Longest Chunked Palindrome Decomposition (1147-adjacent) use hashes to compare halves in O(1).
  7. Number of Distinct Substrings variants: the count of distinct substrings is n(n+1)/2 minus the sum of the suffix array’s LCP values. Suffix arrays are beyond most interviews, but knowing the formula is a nice touch.
  8. Base choice. Use a prime base larger than the alphabet (131, 137, 1000003) and a large prime modulus (10^9 + 7, 2^61 - 1). Using base = 26 with a small modulus collides immediately on English text.
  9. Find All Anagrams in a String (438) and Permutation in String (567) are solved with a frequency rolling window, not a polynomial hash — the 26-element count array is the right tool there. Recognise which rolling technique the alphabet size suggests.
  10. Recognition signal. ‘Longest repeated substring’, ‘count distinct substrings’, ‘check if two substrings are equal many times’, or any problem where the constraints require better than O(n^2) substring comparison.

Part XV · The Hard Core
Chapter 85

Divide and Conquer

The Kernel

Split the input in half, solve both halves, combine. The combine step is where the algorithm lives — and for counting problems, the combine step is a merge that also counts inversions.

31
Problems mapped
3
Easy
19
Medium
9
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The merge-sort-with-counting template. Sort the array while counting cross-half pairs. Count of Smaller Numbers After Self (315), Reverse Pairs (493) and Count of Range Sum (327) are all the same code with a different comparison in the merge step. Learn one, get three.
  2. The counting must happen before the merge, using the fact that both halves are already sorted. Two pointers walk the halves and count pairs satisfying the predicate; then the standard merge proceeds. If you count during the merge you lose the sortedness guarantee.
  3. Count of Range Sum (327) is the hardest of the three because the predicate is a range (lower <= sum <= upper), which needs two pointers rather than one. The prefix-sum transformation is the first step.
  4. Maximum Subarray divide and conquer (53): best in the left, best in the right, best crossing the midpoint (computed with a suffix scan and a prefix scan). O(n log n), and the same shape as 315.
  5. Different Ways to Add Parentheses (241) and Unique Binary Search Trees II (95) are divide-and-conquer enumeration: split at every operator or root, recurse both sides, combine the results. The memoisation on the interval is what makes 241 polynomial.
  6. Median of Two Sorted Arrays (4) is divide and conquer on the partition, not the array (chapter 14). Recognise that ‘divide’ can mean ‘divide the answer space’.
  7. Sort List (148) is merge sort on a linked list (chapter 36). Sort an Array (912) should be merge sort or heap sort if the interviewer forbids the built-in — quicksort’s worst case is O(n^2).
  8. Beautiful Array (932) is the classic construction by parity recursion: A(n) = 2 A(ceil(n/2)) - 1 + 2 A(floor(n/2)). The recursion on the structure rather than the data is unusual and worth seeing once.
  9. Expression Add Operators (282) and Different Ways to Add Parentheses are both ‘enumerate the splits’. When a problem says ‘add parentheses’, think divide and conquer.
  10. Master theorem. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) is O(n log n); T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) is O(n); T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) is O(log n). Being able to state the recurrence and its solution is expected.
  11. Recursion depth. Divide and conquer on n = 10^5 gives depth log2(10^5) ≈ 17, which is safe. But a skewed split (e.g. always splitting at index 0) gives depth n and will raise RecursionError. Check that your split is balanced.

Chapter 86

Quickselect and Partitioning

The Kernel

Partition around a pivot, then recurse into only the side that contains your answer. Expected O(n), worst case O(n^2) — which is exactly what the interviewer will ask about.

17
Problems mapped
4
Easy
13
Medium
0
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Lomuto partition. Choose a pivot, then one pass swapping elements smaller than the pivot to the front. Returns the pivot’s final index. Simple but degrades to O(n^2) on sorted input with a first/last pivot.
  2. Randomised pivot. random.randint(lo, hi) before partitioning makes the expected complexity O(n) regardless of input order. Saying ‘I randomise the pivot to avoid the adversarial worst case’ is the answer to the follow-up question.
  3. Quickselect. After partitioning, if the pivot index equals k, return; if k < pivot_index, recurse left; else recurse right. Recurse into one side only — that is what makes it O(n) expected rather than O(n log n).
  4. Kth Largest Element in an Array (215) is the archetype. The index conversion: the kth largest is the (n - k)th smallest. Get this wrong and you are off by one.
  5. K Closest Points to Origin (973) and Top K Frequent Elements (347) are quickselect with a different key. Both also have heap solutions (chapter 30); the heap is O(n log k) and the quickselect is O(n) expected. Offer both and let the interviewer choose.
  6. Wiggle Sort II (324) needs the median via quickselect and then a three-way partition. It is the hardest application in this chapter.
  7. Sort Colors (75) is the three-way (Dutch national flag) partition in one pass: three pointers for 0, 1, 2. Memorise it — it is the most-asked partition problem and it is six lines.
  8. Move Zeroes (283) and Remove Element (27) are the one-way partition from chapter 6 — a degenerate case worth recognising as such.
  9. Three-way partition (elements < pivot, == pivot, > pivot) is what makes quicksort fast on duplicate-heavy input. Mention it when asked about quicksort’s behaviour on many duplicates.
  10. Quickselect vs heap: the decision. If k is small relative to n, use a heap of size k (O(n log k), and it streams). If k is arbitrary and the data is in memory, quickselect is O(n) expected. State the trade-off rather than picking blindly.
  11. The worst case. Quickselect’s O(n^2) happens when every partition is maximally unbalanced. With a random pivot the probability is negligible; with a median-of-medians pivot it is O(n) guaranteed, but the constant is large and it is almost never worth implementing. Knowing that median-of-medians exists is the answer to ‘can you guarantee it?’

Chapter 87

Randomized Algorithms and Reservoir Sampling

The Kernel

Reservoir sampling picks a uniformly random element from a stream of unknown length in O(1) space: keep the i-th element with probability 1/i.

14
Problems mapped
0
Easy
11
Medium
3
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Reservoir sampling, memorised. res = first; for i, x in enumerate(stream[1:], 2): if random.randint(1, i) == 1: res = x. Each element is kept with probability 1/n, so the result is uniform.
  2. Linked List Random Node (382) is reservoir sampling over a linked list — you cannot know the length in advance, which is exactly the sampling problem’s premise.
  3. Random Pick Index (398) is reservoir sampling over the matching indices only. The count i must increment only when the value matches.
  4. Shuffle an Array (384) is Fisher-Yates: for i in range(n-1, 0, -1): j = randint(0, i); a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]. Iterate from the end and swap with an index in [0, i]. Swapping forward, or picking j from [0, n-1], produces a non-uniform distribution — that is the standard trap.
  5. Random Pick with Weight (528) is a prefix-sum plus bisect on a random draw in [0, total). bisect_right is the correct variant — it handles the boundary where the draw lands exactly on a prefix sum.
  6. Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) (380) is chapter 24’s swap-with-last trick. Randomized Collection (381) extends it to duplicates with a dict of sets.
  7. Randomized Set and friends are design problems, not probability problems — the randomness is trivial and the data-structure engineering is the difficulty.
  8. Uniformity is the thing being tested. For every problem in this chapter, be ready to argue that each outcome has equal probability. 'Each element survives with probability 1/i at step i, so the probability of surviving to the end is 1/n' is the standard argument.
  9. Implement Rand10() Using Rand7() (470) is rejection sampling: generate a uniform number in a range that is a multiple of 10 and reject the rest. The expected number of calls is constant. It is a favourite problem at large companies and is purely about the sampling argument.
  10. Python specifics. Use random.randint(a, b) for inclusive integer ranges and random.random() for floats. random.choice is uniform over a sequence. random.shuffle is Fisher-Yates already — do not reimplement it unless asked.
  11. Recognition signal. ‘Uniformly at random’, ‘each element equally likely’, ‘without knowing the length in advance’, or a stream you cannot store. Also: any design problem where the query is ‘give me a random one’.

Hard Design Problems – The Composite Round

The Kernel

Every hard design problem is two or three earlier templates bolted together. Name the templates out loud before you write a line of code; that naming is the interview.

92
Problems mapped
8
Easy
60
Medium
24
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. LRU Cache (146) = hash map + doubly linked list with sentinels (chapter 24). LFU Cache (460) = hash map + per-frequency ordered lists + a min_freq counter. Both must be O(1) per operation; if your solution walks a structure, it is not finished.
  2. Design Twitter (355) = per-user tweet lists + a follow set + a heap merge for the feed. The feed is Merge k Sorted Lists (chapter 32) in a design costume.
  3. Range Module (715) = a sorted list of disjoint intervals plus bisect for insertion. Every operation is ‘find the overlapping range, merge, reinsert’. It is chapter 18’s merge applied incrementally.
  4. My Calendar I/II/III (729, 731, 732) = a sorted container of intervals, or a sweep line with a count. 732 (max concurrent bookings) is a difference-array / ordered-map problem — a plain dict of deltas plus a running maximum on demand is not O(1) per query, so you need an ordered structure or a sorted list with bisect.
  5. Snapshot Array (1146) = per-index (snap_id, value) history plus a global counter, with bisect for the lookup (chapter 24).
  6. Time Based Key-Value Store (981) = per-key parallel lists of timestamps and values, with bisect_right (chapter 24).
  7. Design Authentication Manager (1797) = dict of token to expiry with lazy expiration. Lazy beats eager: never run a timer, just check on access.
  8. Design a Food Rating System (2353) = dict of cuisines to a heap of (-rating, food, version), with version numbers for lazy deletion. Lazy deletion by version stamp is the reusable trick whenever the underlying structure cannot be mutated efficiently.
  9. Stock Price Fluctuation (2034) = dict of timestamp to price plus two heaps (max and min) with lazy deletion by comparing against the current dict. Same trick.
  10. Design Skiplist (1206) and All O(1) Data Structure (432) are the hardest in the chapter. 1206 asks you to implement a probabilistic balanced structure — if asked, implement it as a layered linked list with random promotion. 432 needs a doubly linked list of buckets plus two hash maps (key to bucket, count to bucket).
  11. Design In-Memory File System (588) = a nested dict with sorted listing. It is a trie by another name.
  12. Encode and Decode TinyURL (535) and Design HashMap (706) are the warm-ups. 535 is a counter plus base-62 encoding; do not invent hashing.
  13. Design Hit Counter (362) = a queue or a ring buffer of 300 buckets. The ring buffer avoids unbounded memory and is the better answer.
  14. The universal method for this chapter. (1) List the operations and their required complexities. (2) Choose one data structure per complexity requirement. (3) State the invariant that links them. (4) Write the helpers first, the public methods second. (5) Test the edge cases: empty structure, single element, delete-then-get.
  15. The most common failure in a design interview is starting to code before naming the structures. Spend two minutes on the whiteboard drawing the boxes and arrows; it converts a 60-line struggle into a 25-line derivation.

Part XVI · Specialist Patterns
Chapter 89

Trie (Prefix Tree)

The Kernel

A tree where each edge is a character and each node is a prefix. It turns ‘does any word start with this prefix’ from O(total length) into O(prefix length).

36
Problems mapped
3
Easy
18
Medium
15
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. The node, memorised. children = {} plus is_end = False. A dict beats a 26-array when the alphabet is large or sparse; a 26-list beats a dict when the alphabet is exactly lowercase and speed matters. Say which you are choosing and why.
  2. Three operations. insert: walk/create children, mark is_end. search: walk, return is_end at the end. startsWith: walk, return True if the walk succeeded. The only difference between search and startsWith is the final is_end check — that is the whole reason Trie has two methods.
  3. Design Add and Search Words (211) adds '.' as a wildcard, which turns the walk into a DFS over all children at that position. The recursion is any(search(node.child[c], i+1) for c in node.children).
  4. Word Search II (212) is the flagship combination: build a Trie of all words, then do a single DFS over the grid that walks the Trie in lockstep. Prune matched words from the Trie as you go (or mark them collected) so the same word is not emitted twice. This is the single best example in the book of a data structure eliminating a nested loop: it takes the problem from O(words cells 4^L) to O(cells * 4^L).
  5. Replace Words (648) walks the Trie and returns the first is_end it hits. The ‘shortest prefix wins’ requirement is satisfied by the walk order — no comparison needed.
  6. Map Sum Pairs (677) stores a running sum at each node, so a prefix query is a single walk. Storing an aggregate per node is the general technique for prefix-sum queries.
  7. Search Suggestions System (1268) needs the top-3 lexicographic matches per prefix. Two options: store a sorted list (or a heap of 3) at each node, or binary-search the sorted word list per prefix. The Trie-with-cached-results version is the intended answer.
  8. Longest Word in Dictionary (720) and Long Encoding of Words (820) use the Trie to test ‘is every prefix also a word’.
  9. Stream of Characters (1032) walks the Trie backwards from the newest character — the query string grows on the left. Recognising that the insertion point is the left end is the difficulty.
  10. The bitwise Trie. Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (421) and Maximum XOR With an Element From Array (1707) build a Trie over the 32 bits of each number, most significant bit first, and greedily take the opposite bit at each level. The greedy is correct because a difference at a higher bit always outweighs all lower bits combined — state that argument.
  11. Palindrome Pairs (336) combines a Trie with a palindrome check per node. It is the hardest Trie problem in the book.
  12. Complexity. Building is O(total characters). Each query is O(query length). Space is O(total characters * branching). Compare against a hash set: a hash set answers exact lookup in O(len) but cannot answer ‘starts with’ at all — that capability is what you are paying space for, and saying so is the answer to ‘why not a hash set?’.

Chapter 90

Eulerian Paths, Bridges, and Advanced Graph Construction

The Kernel

Hierholzer’s algorithm finds an Eulerian path by DFS-ing edges and appending nodes in postorder, then reversing. It is the answer to ‘use every edge exactly once’.

22
Problems mapped
2
Easy
12
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Hierholzer, memorised. def dfs(u): while adj[u]: v = adj[u].pop(); dfs(v); route.append(u). Then reverse route. The append happens after the recursion — that postorder placement is the entire algorithm and is the thing candidates get wrong.
  2. Existence condition. An Eulerian path exists iff at most two nodes have odd degree (and the graph is connected on its non-isolated nodes). An Eulerian circuit exists iff every node has even degree. State this before writing code — it is the conceptual half of the answer.
  3. Reconstruct Itinerary (332) is Hierholzer with two twists: the adjacency lists must be sorted in reverse so that pop() yields the lexicographically smallest next hop, and the answer is the reversed postorder. The reversed-sort trick is the whole difficulty.
  4. Valid Arrangement of Pairs (2097) is the same algorithm with an explicit start-node computation: find the node with out_degree - in_degree == 1, or any node if all degrees balance.
  5. Cracking the Safe (753) is Eulerian on a de Bruijn graph: nodes are (k-1)-length strings, edges are k-length strings. Recognising that the problem is ‘find an Eulerian circuit in a de Bruijn graph’ is the entire solution, and it is a genuinely beautiful reduction.
  6. Bridges and articulation points (Tarjan). Critical Connections in a Network (1192) needs the disc/low arrays: an edge (u, v) is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u]. The DFS with a parent parameter and the back-edge update low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]) is the template. Memorise the low[v] > disc[u] test — it is the bridge criterion.
  7. Minimum Number of Days to Disconnect Island (1568) and Minimum Number of Vertices to Reach All Nodes (1557) are connectivity-edge cases; 1568's answer is always 0, 1 or 2, and proving that bound is the interesting part.
  8. Strongly connected components (Kosaraju, Tarjan) rarely appear in interviews but Critical Connections uses the same low-link idea. Know the name.
  9. Minimum Spanning Tree. Kruskal = sort edges + Union-Find (chapter 55). Prim = grow from a node with a min-heap. Min Cost to Connect All Points (1584) is Kruskal; Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost (1135) is the same. 1489 Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges requires running Kruskal several times with forced/excluded edges — a good test of whether you understand the algorithm rather than just memorised it.
  10. Graph construction problems. Find if Path Exists in Graph (1971), Keys and Rooms (841), Find the Town Judge (997), Find the Celebrity (277), Kill Process (582) and Clone Graph (133) are all ‘build the adjacency structure, then traverse’. The difficulty is almost always in the construction, not the traversal — and 277 has an O(n) elimination solution that avoids building anything.
  11. Time Needed to Inform All Employees (1376) is a tree DFS with a parent array instead of child pointers — recognising that a parent array is a tree is a common interview reduction.
  12. Alien Dictionary (269) and Sequence Reconstruction (444) are topological sort with derived edges (chapter 54).

Chapter 91

Computational Geometry Basics

The Kernel

Three tools: the cross product for orientation, the squared distance for comparisons, and monotone-chain convex hull. Almost every geometry problem is one of those three.

30
Problems mapped
8
Easy
14
Medium
8
Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Cross product orientation. For points a, b, c, cross = (b.x - a.x) (c.y - a.y) - (b.y - a.y) (c.x - a.x). Positive means counter-clockwise, negative means clockwise, zero means collinear. Memorise this one formula — it answers ‘is this a straight line’, ‘is this polygon convex’, and ‘do these segments cross’.
  2. Check If It Is a Straight Line (1232) is ‘all cross products zero’. Valid Boomerang (1037) is ‘cross product non-zero’. Convex Polygon (469) is ‘all cross products the same sign’.
  3. Erect the Fence (587) is the monotone chain convex hull: sort points, build the lower hull by popping while the cross product turns clockwise, then the upper hull, then concatenate. The while pop condition is cross(hull[-2], hull[-1], p) <= 0 for counter-clockwise hulls, and the <= versus < decides whether collinear points are kept. LeetCode’s test cases care about collinear points on the boundary, so use <=.
  4. Squared distances, never square roots. K Closest Points to Origin (973), Largest Triangle Area (812) and every ‘nearest/farthest’ geometry problem compare dxdx + dydy. Using math.hypot introduces floating-point error and is slower.
  5. Max Points on a Line (149) normalises each slope fraction by gcd(dy, dx) so it can be hashed. The normalisation must handle the sign consistently (e.g. force dx > 0, or dx == 0 with dy > 0) or the same line produces two different keys. That sign rule is the whole problem.
  6. Rectangle Area (223) and Rectangle Overlap (836) are inclusion-exclusion on axis-aligned rectangles: the intersection width is max(0, min(x2) - max(x1)). The max(0, ...) clamp is what handles non-overlap and is the standard bug.
  7. Rectangle Area II (850) and Perfect Rectangle (391) require coordinate compression or a sweep line with a segment tree — they are the hard end of this chapter.
  8. Surface Area of 3D Shapes (892) and Projection Area (883) are counting arguments on a grid, not geometry. Recognise them and skip the machinery.
  9. Minimum Area Rectangle (939) is a hash-set problem: for each pair of points forming a diagonal, test whether the other two corners exist. O(n^2) with a set, no geometry needed.
  10. Floating point. Never test a == b for floats. Use abs(a - b) < 1e-9. For geometry, prefer integer arithmetic via cross products so you never leave the integers at all — that is the mark of a careful answer.
  11. Best Meeting Point (296) is a median problem: the Manhattan distance is minimised at the median of each coordinate independently. Separability of the coordinates is the insight — it applies to any Manhattan-metric problem.
  12. Recognition signal. ‘Points’, ‘lines’, ‘rectangles’, ‘area’, ‘perimeter’, ‘collinear’, ‘convex’. For Manhattan distance, think median or a coordinate transform; for Euclidean, think cross product and squared distance.

Concurrency (Where It Still Appears)

The Kernel

LeetCode’s concurrency track is a separate skill from algorithms. In Python interviews it appears rarely, but the primitives are worth knowing by name.

Hard

The Boundary Rules

  1. Print in Order (1114) is a chained-lock problem: first releases second, second releases third. Each thread waits on its own lock.
  2. Print FooBar Alternately (1115) is two threads alternating on two locks — the classic hand-off pattern.
  3. Print Zero Even Odd (1116) is a three-way hand-off with a shared counter.
  4. Building H2O (1117) uses a Barrier and a Semaphore to enforce the 2:1 ratio.
  5. Design Bounded Blocking Queue (1188) is a queue with two semaphores (slots and items) or a Condition.
  6. The Dining Philosophers (1226) is the classic deadlock problem; the fix is an ordering rule on lock acquisition (always pick the lower-numbered fork first).
  7. Python specifics. threading.Lock, threading.Semaphore, threading.Barrier, threading.Condition, and queue.Queue (which is already thread-safe) are the tools. Python’s GIL means threads do not give CPU parallelism — they give concurrency for I/O. Saying that is often the most valuable sentence in a concurrency discussion.
  8. When this chapter matters. It matters for interviews at companies that run real systems rounds, and it matters for the system-design portion of a loop. It is not part of the standard algorithm loop at most companies — if you are short on time, read this chapter’s boundary rules and move on.
  9. The transferable skill is not the LeetCode exercises but the habit of asking: what is shared mutable state, what is the lock that protects it, and what is the lock-acquisition order that prevents deadlock.
